utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [B/C/S on English channel]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we'll start our hearings again this Thursday, 16th of August. I want to welcome all the present in the courtroom. The Prosecution, the counsel -- [B/C/S on English channel]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It should be resolved now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I hear French interpretation, English, and B/C/S. Apparently everything is working. So I was saying that we are starting our hearings again, and I am welcoming all those present. As you know, we have a witness, which is coming for two days. As for the schedule, today we are sitting until 1.00, and we will resume at a quarter past 2.00 until 7.00 p.m. For the orderly continuation we will continue until 10.45. We will have a break of 30 minutes, and we will resume and go until a quarter past 2.00. Originally the Prosecution had provided for -- for the document. The Prosecution could maybe in three hours finish the -- finish the examination-in-chief. The Defence will need three hours, or each accused. If the Prosecution needs more than three hours we will allot more time to the Defence, of course. So this is what I can now indicate. Also, during the summer recess, I was told that for reasons which have to do with the other trials and interpreters' problems, we will not be in a position next week to sit on Tuesday and Wednesday because other trials have been scheduled. And also, Monday there was to be a witness who is not coming on Monday. Next week we have no hearings on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday, but we do sit on Thursday, and the week after we have also been told that on Wednesday we couldn't sit because there's another trial. I'm very sorry about all that, but this was for me a fait accompli. Presently there are seven trials which are ongoing for three courtrooms only. Therefore, normally with the turnover some hearings will have to be postponed or cancelled. We are now going to see the new witness, and before the examination-in-chief starts, Mrs. Usher, could you go and get the witness. Yes, Mr. Coric. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I have a request to make. At the stage when my Defence team is being replaced we had two ex parte sessions. Since after that my former Defence counsel has made several appearances -- MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour. Maybe we should move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Closed session. Just a moment, Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell us your name, first name, and birth date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Larry Charles Forbes. My birth date is September 20, 1949.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your profession today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm retired from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police after 36 years of service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified at this Tribunal or is it the first time you come as a witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like you to read the declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You can sit down. A few explanations are in order for this hearing. Since you are a mounted police, an ex-mounted police from Canada, you know about the proceedings when witness are being heard. First you will have to answer questions which will be asked by the Prosecution on your right hand and which you already met in order to proof and prepare this hearing. Once these questions will have been asked, counsel from the Defence which are on your left, perhaps even the accused, may ask you some questions within the framework of cross-examination. The three Judges which you can see in front of you may at any time also ask questions from you, but we prefer as much as possible wait until both parties have finished asking questions to ask our own questions. If at any time you don't feel well, don't hesitate. Let us know. We have pauses every hour and a half for about 20 minutes in general, and today we are supposed to hear your testimony today and tomorrow morning. In general, this is the explanations I wanted to give to you on the way this hearing will go on, especially for your testimony it. So I now give the floor to the Prosecution, whom I also greet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning to Defence counsel and to everybody else in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Forbes?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I think you just told Their Honours you're a retired member of the RCMP?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe for us your training and your background within that service, please.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I joined the Royal Canadian Mounted Police at Fredricton, New Brunswick and I immediately was sent to Regina, Saskatchewan to start my basic training. I had six months of basic training in Regina, Saskatchewan and then was posted to an isolated northern detachment in Manitoba which was only accessible by air or by train. I finished six months of field training there and then another six months on detachment, and I was transferred to Ottawa, our nation's capital, and at Ottawa I was on three months of equestrian training learning to ride. At the end of that I was transferred back to northern Manitoba where I worked in Thompson city and Flin Flon city detachments doing general city policing, general police work. At the end of that, I was transferred to Winnipeg Manitoba, the capital city of Manitoba and the largest city in Manitoba, where I worked on assistance investigations for outlying detachments and also on warrant detail. I then was assigned to highway patrol duties on the outskirts of Winnipeg for 10 months doing general traffic duties, and then I was transferred to our customs and excise section in Winnipeg, which was a five-year posting, plain clothes investigations of smuggling into Canada but also involved some smuggling out of Canada. Most of the things that I worked on involved the smuggling of guns, liquor, and pornography. Just before going on to that section I should mention that I spent a time on a public relations unit, the centennial mounted unit for Manitoba, which was basically riding my horse in my dress uniform of boots and breaches, red tunic and Stetson as public relations for the RCMP. At the end of my five year posting in customs and excise, I was transferred to a smaller rural town south of Winnipeg, a farming community, and I did rural policing there for three months, general police duties -- pardon me for three years, Your Honours. At the end of that I was transferred to Selkirk detachment which is a small city north of Winnipeg, and I was stationed there for six years, and I worked on the municipal detachment doing city policing and on also on the rural detachment doing policing outside the town. At that time, too, I'd also taken a course I'd applied and was accepted and passed the undercover operator's course. And so during -- from that time I -- I passed my course in the fall of 1985 and from 1985 besides my other duties, I was an undercover operator and would be called on numerous times to work undercover all across the country. I was fortunate enough to do about 30 undercover operations, and I got to work in every province in Canada from coast-to-coast except for Newfoundland.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can I ask you there, did there come a time when you decided to volunteer for overseas service?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct. I volunteered -- I was already transferred from Selkirk into Winnipeg into a specialised unit doing VIP security and explosives disposal, and it was when I was in Winnipeg that I had the opportunity to volunteer to work with the United Nations in peacekeeping duties in the former Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly request both counsel and witness to speak more slowly and observe pauses between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: In what capacity did you volunteer for the United Nations service?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: To work for a six-month tour with UN CIVPOL as a civilian police monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you undergo any training for the mission prior to your deployment?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, once I was accepted we were sent to Ottawa for a week where we had a week's briefings and also attended to administrative needs that we would need for the mission, and -- but basically it was just a week's -- a week's training and what we could expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you remember when you actually arrived to the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes. I arrived in Zagreb on the 25th of August -- pardon me, on the 25th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And when you arrived there did you receive further training or briefings?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes. We had a couple of days of briefings in Zagreb, and then I was transferred down to Sector South. I went to Knin and just spent one day there overnight and then I went to Gracac, and I was stationed there until the -- I was transferred to Mostar station on the 28th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, can you describe for us the structure of UNCIVPOL as it existed at the time of your arrival to the Balkans in 1993 starting from the top down if you would, please.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir. At the top the CIVPOL was broken down into five sectors being east, west, north and south and sector Sarajevo. In headquarters Zagreb the commissioner for CIVPOL at that time was a Canadian mounted policeman by the name of O'Reilly, and he was overall in charge. They would have also a deputy commissioner there. They would have an administrative officer, an operations officer, a duty officer, all with respective areas of responsibility. Each of the sections or -- each of the sections was organised much the same way with a section commander in charge. They would have an administrative officer, operations officer, et cetera, and then the sectors were broken down into stations, and there would be a number of stations. When I went to sector Sarajevo, there were only three CIVPOL stations within Sector Sarajevo. One was in Srebrenica, one was in Mostar, and the other one was in Sarajevo itself. Each station or detachment would have the station commander and would also have a deputy commander, an operations officer, an admin officer, depending on the size of the station and the number of manpower they had there. When I went to -- first arrived at Mostar station, I was the operations -- made the operations officer in charge of investigations and the liaison officer for East Mostar, and I -- I was also later on became the deputy commander of Mostar station.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Just for the record, we've been referring to UNCIVPOL, the acronym UNCIVPOL. What was the complete name for it?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: United Nations Civil Police Monitors, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell us what was the mandate or function of UNCIVPOL or United Nations Civil Police?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Their mandate were to monitor the local police in the areas that they would be stationed in to make sure that the minority in that particular area. At that time basically everywhere in the former Yugoslavia one of either the Croatians, the Serbs, or in Bosnia the Bosnian Muslims controlled an area and there would be minorities of the other groups of people in each of those, and the job of CIVPOL was to accompany the police on their patrols and to make sure that the minorities in the area were treated fairly and humanely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: In the course of the CIVPOL duties did you work independently or with other UN agencies?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: We worked quite closely with other United Nations agencies. We worked very closely with civilian affairs, UNHCR, also International Red Cross, and the military UNMOs and whatever battalion happened to be in the area that you were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did part of your duties overlap with those other agencies in terms of perhaps identifying humanitarian needs for groups of people affected by conflict?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. You would -- if you identified a need you would have of course pass on that information to the agency that was best able to help out in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you were posted to Mostar at the end of June 1998. Were you actually based in the city of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, sir. On arriving at Mostar we lived in the town of Medjugorje south-west of the city of Mostar. At that time Medjugorje was in control of the Bosnian Croats, and on arriving at Medjugorje it -- the town was -- you would never know that there was a war going on in a lot of regards. There was no damage or anything like that there, and this is where we stayed when -- and patrolled out of from Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what was the distance between Mostar and Medjugorje? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: It would be approximately -- I would estimate it to be about 30 kilometres. It sometimes took quite a long time to actually get there, and so I'm not really certain on the physical distance, but I would -- I would estimate 30 to 35 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what was the actual area of responsibility attached to the -- the station of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Well, because of the war situation in Mostar, we weren't able to carry out regular patrols and to go with the police and carry out our regular mandate as such, and when I became able to enter into East Mostar and become the liaison officer there, because of the war situation I had to go in in an armoured vehicle, stay overnight in the armoured vehicle and --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: We'll come to that in a moment, but I'm just interested to know the specific area of responsibility, the area of the Mostar station.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: You have East Mostar. Was there another area?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the station itself was responsible for all of the area around Mostar that we could get access to and so that was mainly all of the area to the south and west of Mostar and Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And were there other UN organisations and organisations based in Medjugorje or nearby Medjugorje?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir, there was. The United Nations battalion that was stationed there were a Spanish Battalion, and the Colonel in charge was a Colonel Morales. There was an UNHCR office there as well, and I believe the gentleman that was in charge of that was Mr. Jerry Hume. There was a civil affairs unit stationed in Medjugorje, and there was Mr. Albert Benabou, there was a Mr. David Joseph, and there was another gentleman, an Irish gentleman. I can't think of his name right now, but the three of them. There was also UNHCR -- or, pardon me, there was also International Red Cross representatives in Medjugorje as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And would it be correct to say that you had regular dealings with these agencies?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Who was your station commander in charge of the Mostar station in the Medjugorje station when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: When I arrived it was Mr. Leo Sorensen from Denmark.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you receive a briefing from Mr. Sorensen about what the position was on the ground in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes I did. In general terms he advised me that the HVO or the Bosnian Croats controlled all of the area around Mostar, on the east side of the river in East Mostar the BiH or Bosnian Muslim forces controlled that, and they also had a small foothold in a few little pockets on the west side of the Neretva River in Mostar, and they were basically surrounded in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So as I understand it, you had largely -- you had largely Croatian forces on the western side, Muslims on the eastern side. Who was situate to the north and who was situate to the south if anybody?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: There was Croatian forces to the north. Further north I understood that there were Serbian forces. However, I never came into contact with any Serbian forces once I left the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And to the south?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: And to the south that was all Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And as you say --

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: -- effectively the Bosnian Muslim forces situate in Mostar were surrounded?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, did you have a reporting system when you were working from the station in Mostar or in Medjugorje and, if so, could you indicate to whom reports were made and how that worked?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The -- the system was when you received a complaint and you started an investigation or an incident came up that you investigated and took part in you would make a complete report on that which would -- a copy of that would be kept at the -- at the station or detachment. A copy would go to the sector headquarters, in our case being Sarajevo, and a copy would go -- would eventually end up at headquarters in Zagreb if it was important enough. There was also a daily sitrep report that each CIVPOL station compiled, much like a daily occurrence report, very -- just -- just the very basic facts. This would be -- usually it was sent in by telephone to the sector headquarters or to the Zagreb headquarters. When I first arrived in Mostar station, a lot of our reports only went directly to Zagreb because of the difficulty of getting things into Sarajevo at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And the reports that you mentioned earlier about where you would be taking reports of complaints, what were the titles of those reports? What were they known as?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: The -- the one was known as a sitrep is the one I've just described which is very brief reports that would be sent in daily as I say mainly by telephone. The other reports would be the incident reports which would be more detailed, and they would be written and delivered by mail if possible. Later on as I got involved in more serious investigations in East Mostar, it was decided that my reports for security reasons would have to be hand-delivered to Sarajevo, which meant that I would have to go to Sarajevo once a week via Split, fly in from Split to deliver the reports. I would overnight at the PTT building in Sarajevo and then return the same route back to Medjugorje and Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I wonder if at this stage with the assistance of the usher I could present to the witness the binder of documents which I have prepared.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Mr. Forbes, for the benefit of the Court I wonder if you could turn to Exhibit 05009 on the binder of documents which I have before you.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Did you say 05, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: It should be marked there as 5009. For the record it will be 05009.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what we apparently have there is a document titled "Incident Report"?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And on the second line of the tabulated indication at the top you have -- it's dated the 13th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And to the right of that CIVPOL name Larry Forbes?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Does this incident that this is an incident report prepared by you?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And perhaps you could just take us through it very, very quickly, the first page, and indicate what -- how it's laid out?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The format you fill in the blanks basically on the top part here dealing with if the person might have been a victim, a complainant, a witness, a suspect and in this particular case it's other, and underlined as other, and it was Mr. Zamo Maslesa. He was the chief of the BiH police in East Mostar. The second one was deputy chief of police, Mr. Salko Zuljevic, deputy chief of police in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And moving on down we find that there's a brief summary --

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: -- of what the report contains?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And then the following pages - and I don't propose to go into them at this point in time - but the following pages, am I correct in saying that these would be the expanded version of the report, a more detailed -- more detail of what the summary contained?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And were all the incidents reports prepared in this format?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And are these reports that you yourself drafted on an independent basis or in collaboration with your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: These ones with my name on them would be -- would have been prepared by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell me when -- when these incident reports were usually drawn up?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: These would be drawn up as soon as I would be able to get back to Medjugorje and be able to sit down at the computer to do -- to type them up. And it was normally -- if it wasn't the same day, if I got back fairly late, it might be the next day, but it wouldn't be any more than -- than overnight before they were completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And the contents of the reports would be based on your recollection of events during your mission to Mostar that day or the previous number of days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And the originals where did they go?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: The originals say eventually -- originals stayed on detachment copies went to headquarters and to the sector headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And often times originals would contain statements, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct. And they would eventually - the original handwritten statements I understood - would eventually end up in Zagreb headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned it briefly but the two principal protagonists in Mostar at the time were the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. I was told that before I arrived that the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims had been on the same side in fighting against the Serbs, and once the Serbs were driven from the area then the -- the Bosnian Croats attacked the Bosnian Muslims and they became -- they began fighting with one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And as a result of that attack, what were the consequences for the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I just want to make sure that we understand each other here. Now the Prosecution is trying to elicit testimony as if this is the gentleman's understanding, this is what the gentleman was told, so perhaps he could preface the questions with what were your told because obviously this is pure hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, I think when you arrived first you were given a general briefing by your senior officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And from what you're telling us at the present, are you telling us on the basis of what you had been told? Are you telling us on what you know from personal experience?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: As far as the fighting between the -- with the Serbs that had taken place before I arrived, and I was just from, what I was told, I have no direct knowledge of that fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, you said that most of your work was in East Mostar, with whom --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand it's inconvenient for the Prosecution to go back, but he indicated that he was told that the Croats attacked the Muslims. Now, that's hearsay. Obviously something happened before his arrival. Now, it begs a few questions, you know, what happened, what did he learn, who did he learn it from.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, I will deal with it later when he is in a better position to deal with it from having spent time on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: As I was asking, you said most of you work in -- was in East Mostar. With whom on the local level did you have contact?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I had contact with the BiH police, usually with either the chief of police or the deputy chief of police, and in some cases with a Mr. Sejic [phoen], who is chief of detectives for East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you remember the name of the chief of police?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, that was Mr. Zamo Maslesa and the deputy chief of police, that was Mr. Salko Zuljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And had both of these men been present in Mostar when the conflict had started as between the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you get further briefing and information from these officers who had been on the ground?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes I did, and also from civilians that I spoke to in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And while I know it's hearsay, can you tell us what in general terms you were informed had happened, when you were informed by the chief of police, had happened in Mostar at the time the conflict started?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I was told that the BiH had been attacked. It was a surprise. A lot of the Muslim policemen who were over on the west side were captured and taken prisoner or had ended shot or whatever in the fighting. Deputy Chief Zuljevic, he had been over on the west side, and he had come over and was visiting with friends on the east side then night when the trouble started, and he told me at one point that that was the reason he wasn't probably captured right off the start.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were you told what consequences the conflict had for the Bosnian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn, you're saying that Zuljevic told you but Mr. Zuljevic does not speak English. Did you have an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was translated to me by an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the interpreter, was he -- was it a Croatian interpreter or a Muslim-Bosniak interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a Muslim Bosnian, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And in your meetings with the chief of police did he inform you what the consequences for the Bosnian Muslim population were as a result of the conflict which had commenced as between two protagonist forces?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, he had told me that they were surrounded. They were cut off from all supplies. There had been about a two-month period where hardly any food got in whatsoever. He also advised about the water situation, there being almost no potable water available. And also of medical supplies and medicine, and being surrounded as they were, there was -- it was very hard for them to get in any kind of supplies other than through like a mule trail through the mountains, and they were in quite desperate situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you receive any information or were you made aware of any detentions or expulsions that had occurred on the western side?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I was advised that there was groups women and children and old people that were being forced across the line almost on a nightly basis, and over -- I received this information from the BiH police, but also from our UNMO military observers and from civilians that I met and spoke with through an interpreter in East Mostar, and as a result of the conversations with them it wasn't known for sure exactly how many people were forced to cross the line, how many Muslim people were forced to cross the line in this manner, but it was estimated that it was about 2.000 people in the four-month period.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, apart from your contacts with the BiH police, did you have contacts with the Bosnian Croat police or Bosnian Croat military?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I didn't myself, sir. The only time I would have contact with them would be when we would be stopped at a roadblock before -- the first time I was able to go into East Mostar was with the first convoy to get in there in a number of months and that was on the 21st of August, 1993. Before that we had attempted to get into Mostar and to go in through West Mostar, but we were always stopped by the HVO police and turned back.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And how -- how would you normally travel into Mostar if you were attempting -- even when you were attempting to get in?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Well, at this -- the only way I ever got into Mostar except for my very last night, my very last trip into Mostar, East Mostar, was in an Armoured Personnel Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And which forces?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: And that belonged to the United Nations, the Spanish Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And were these personnel carriers distinctively marked?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They were painted white and they had big black letters saying UN on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And which route did you normally take when you were going into Mostar?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: The most common route that we took was to leave from camp Dracevo, which was south of Medjugorje down toward Metkovic, Metkovic, and we could come up the east side of the Neretva River through the Croatian-held territory, crossing over the no man's land at the old airport, and then into the area of East Mostar that was controlled by the BiH forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell us who was in control of the access roads leading into Mostar?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: The Bosnian Croats were in control of all of the access roads going into Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: When you say all of the access roads, did you ever try to take alternative routes in?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And a couple of occasions, we did go up on the west side through Citluk and cross the bridge. They used to refer to it as the broken bridge, and cross over to that side there. I also attempted a couple of times before I was ever successful in getting in to go in through West Mostar, but we were always turned back and couldn't proceed into Mostar that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And who was it that turned you back?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That was the HVO police and in some cases the HVO military.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And were there any reasons given to you for turning you back?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: They would just say that we weren't allowed to go further and no real good explanation why we couldn't. It was just forbidden.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: You mentioned that you would travel in the Spanish Armoured Personnel Carriers. Why was it necessary to travel in these armoured vehicles?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Because of the war situation, sir. There was shelling and sniper fire was quite prevalent. On a number occasions going into East Mostar our -- our APCs were shot at and they also came close to usually high explosives were usually from mortars. And so in order to be safe, we used to batten down the hatches and stay inside until we were through the battle line and into a safe position in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned shelling and sniping. From where was this coming if you know?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It was coming from the west side of the Neretva River in the area of Mount Hum. And also there had been shelling I saw coming from further north and west. There was a lookout in the north-west area of West Mostar on the high ground. There was shelling and shooting coming from there as well. Also, I had noticed on a couple of occasions, and I was able to triangulate where launch sites of rockets were being fired above on the high ground, the west side of the Neretva River, west of Buna, and I was able to fairly accurately plot these shots by observing and taking a compass reading and then moving to a new position, taking another compass reading, doing that a third time and where the readings intercepted -- intersected to give us a fairly accurate position of where the rocket fire had been coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And are you in a position to say where this shooting and shelling was aimed at?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, it was aimed over at East Mostar and the BiH-controlled area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: When you were in East Mostar when you were conducting your duties, did you observe whether or not the shelling and shooting was aimed at military forces?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Most of shooting and shelling that I saw was either indiscriminate, fired into the civilian areas, or and in some cases targeted at ourselves in the UN vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Would this be a frequent occurrence that the UN vehicles would be targeted or would it be a once-off situation?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that it was an everyday occurrence but it did -- it did happen fairly often.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were there any injuries or deaths caused to the UN forces that you're aware of as a result of this shelling or shooting?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir, there were. There was a Spanish lieutenant that was killed just before I arrived in Mostar, and I helped in the investigation of his death. There was also an incident where a number of Spanish soldiers were hit by fragmentation and shrapnel from mortars. I witnessed the UNMOs' house being shelled and I saw -- it actually didn't hit it, the high explosives, but I was in there one night sleeping when the bullets were whacking against the sandbags that protected the west wall of the building and four of them through the night passed over where I was sleeping, and one of them hit a picture of a deer in a painting just above one of the United Nations UNMO -- UNMOs who was from Egypt.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, can I take you back for a moment. You mentioned that there was a Spanish lieutenant killed as a result of the shooting and sniping. Was it known from where the fire had come that had killed him or was it suspected?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, it was, sir. As a result of the investigation that we carried out, at first because of where he was hit, he was hit in the shoulder --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Perhaps you could just explain for the panel, just give a brief description of the incident, what you know of the incident?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Before the witness does that could we have some foundation of what role the witness place in the investigation so that we know what he did and what was relayed to him by others please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: As a result of the killing of the Spanish lieutenant, was there an investigation ordered by your superiors?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, there was, and there was given a special mandate from UN headquarters in New York to carry out the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And were you -- did you receive orders to carry out this investigation with your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes. I wasn't ordered personally but I -- I assisted in the investigation and -- and helped in preparing the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And before we actually deal with that, can you just briefly tell us the circumstances of the lieutenant's death?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes. The lieutenant was a crew chief in one of the United Nations Armoured Personnel Carriers. They were proceeding into East Mostar from West Mostar across the Tito Bridge, and on crossing the Tito bridge he had been hit in a straight stretch there we were able to determine where he was, that it took place in that particular spot, because the driver of the Armoured Personnel Carrier turned around and saw that the lieutenant was standing in the hatch. The driver then had to -- he turned and concentrated on his driving, but just before he had to make a left turn, he glanced back again. And in that short period of time the lieutenant had been hit and had fallen down into the inside of the APC. So we knew that he was hit in a small area -- in a short distance. We were able to say where he -- where he was when -- when the bullet hit him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you went about conducting your investigation?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: From doing interviews with the other crew members in his APC and from the results of the autopsy and the physical evidence of the bullet entrance wound in his flak jacket and where it had exited gave us a bullet path which way had it come from, and what it did come from? At first we thought it may have been an accidental shooting --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to insist, but if the witness is going to be asked to give an opinion or to speculate, I still don't know what part he played in the investigation, what he did as opposed to what he may have been told by others. And I understand that hearsay may be admissible but I think it's important to understand his opinion to know exactly what the witness did personally and what was the result of information he was given by others. Mr. Flynn still hasn't made that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Perhaps you could just expand little bit clearer as to your actual personal involvement. Take it step-by-step detail by detail.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, my personal involvement would be to -- listening to the Spanish soldiers witnesses. The other information regard --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you -- did you take statements from them?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I was there when they were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: But you -- you yourself didn't actually take the statements?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, I didn't sign them I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: But you were present?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And you heard what was said?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct. And also the other information, I didn't do the autopsy myself of course, and the physical evidence was just from what I observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Who was it who conducted the autopsy if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I don't know, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you conduct any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't understand what you're saying. Apparently you were entrusted with an inquiry mission. This is what you've said. How is it possible then that you didn't yourself note statements.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I wasn't the primary investigator in it. I was just there assisting. It was Mr. Sorensen, the deputy commander, who was in charge of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. But did he take statements from the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And were you present at the time he took the statements from the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, for -- from the Spanish soldiers that were in the APC. That was the only witnesses that I was present when --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Apart from the Spanish soldiers, were there statements to your knowledge taken from other people to assist in the investigation?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, I believe there were. They interviewed people on both the BiH side and on the HVO side as to what they saw or what they did, but I had no direct knowledge of that. I just read about the -- read it afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: How many people were in the investigative team?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Altogether there were I would say four.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: And I had a very minor part in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you attend the crime scene, if we want to call it for a better word? Did you conduct a -- did you -- did you conduct an investigation of the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, I didn't personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you go to where the Spanish lieutenant had been shot at any stage?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I didn't personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you know whether any photographs were taken?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, I believe there were photographs taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you see those photographs?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I did see some photographs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were you present or did you see -- were you present when the autopsy was conducted?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, I wasn't sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you see the autopsy report?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: What other expert reports were prepared to assist in this investigation if any?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: The ballistic reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Who was it that prepared those?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I -- I believe it was the -- the HVO were involved in it, and I think Mr. Sorensen was involved in it personally as well, but again I'm not absolutely certain on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you know how long the investigation took place, how long it took to conduct the investigation?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: The entire investigation, no, sir, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you have access to the file, the report file, upon completion of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes. I actually helped write the final report. It was -- I was the only English speaker really, and the language of the mission was English, so I helped with the writing of that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And how did it come about -- how did it come about that since you played such a minor role, in your own words, that you helped to write the report?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: From all of the statements that were before me and from what Mr. Sorensen was explaining to me as we wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you remember what the conclusion of the report was?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: The conclusion of the report was that the Spanish soldier, the Spanish lieutenant, had been shot from above and behind, the bullet coming from fairly high up on the west side of Mostar, from the HVO-controlled area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Could I turn you -- ask you to turn to your booklet of documents, and if you could turn to Exhibit 041 -- 03415, please.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I have that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: The title is: "Subject: Death of 1st Lieutenant Fernandez Francisco, concerning conclusion chief investigation -- investigator Station Commander Leo Bang Sorensen, Detective Chief Inspector."

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Is this the report that was prepared by your team arising from the investigation?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you participate and --

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes. I actually did the typing of it and -- of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And have you read through the report and having read through the report, do you agree with its contents?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes. I haven't read it for 14 years but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I object I object to this. First of all the witness has already said he played a very minor role in the investigation. His participation in preparing the report was apparently because he spoke English and was asked to type it, and I don't recall from Mr. Flynn's introduction of the witness that he has any expertise despite his long police experience in ballistics or crime scene investigation or detective work generally. So, Your Honour, we've already had a great deal of evidence from other witnesses on this subject. We may have more. I submit this -- for this witness to express such an opinion is no value.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I'm merely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we have here a report in front of us which is 3415, signed by Mr. Sorensen, on the 4th of July. According to what you say, you are the one who typed out this report. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When you typed it, you started by saying that on the 11th of June, approximately around 19.35 and so on, is it somebody who is telling you to type that or is it yourself who is typing this from other documents you -- we can see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Mr. Sorensen is there, and he's talk and I'm putting it into the proper English and typing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, what is written here is dictated, is said by Mr. Sorensen, and you're just typing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be fair to say, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And the purpose of presenting this report to this witness is merely to authenticate the report, Your Honour. He had a small part playing in the investigation and he prepared the report, so he's in a position to say that he's the one that prepared the report. It's a matter for the Trial Chamber to decide whether to accept the report and its contents from what is heard already or from other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But that was -- Your Honour, with all due respect to my colleague, and I think we need to be somewhat more intellectually honest with the Trial Chamber. He was asking the gentleman to confirm the conclusion, and in order for the gentleman to do so, he would have to lay a foundation that the gentleman is some sort of an expert. I think Mr. Murphy beat me to the punch when he indicated exactly why the gentleman was not competent to render such an opinion. So to now say that they wanted to merely introduce the report, they could have said that five minutes ago by merely stating is this a report that you typed out based on dictation and that would have been the end of it. Now we that we have to bring in somebody else to interpret this report for the benefit of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We know that this report has been typed by the witness. Mr. Flynn, I'm a bit surprised because in this document I see that there are photographs, and these photographs we don't have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And neither do we, Your Honours. This report in its present form is all that we have. And my purpose was merely to ask the witness to authenticate it. He did play a minor role in the investigation. He was present when soldiers who assisted in the investigation and who were able to clarify the facts gave statements. So he was in a position to give some form of conclusion. He prepared this report, and I believe he is a proper person to authenticate the report. If my colleagues want to argue the contents of the report of course that's a different matter, and I that regret that I'm not in a position to furnish the trial panel with the photographs attached to the report. I don't propose to ask him any further questions in relation to the report, and obviously when I submit the final list of exhibits my colleagues have -- have the right to object to the admission of that exhibit at that stage, and it will be a matter for the trial panel to decide on the facts and what the witness -- what evidence the witness has given and other evidence that has been presented before the Trial Chamber to decide whether to admit this or not to admit it. Perhaps the best thing would be to move on from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can continue. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So you have spoken about this officer's death, and you also gave us some other examples in which UNPROFOR -- UNPROFOR forces were targeted. Was there a bad relationship existing between the HVO and UN agencies?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes. It was -- I believe that they felt that -- because we were trying to take in supplies of food and humanitarian relief to the BiH that we were assisting their enemy, and so as a result we were not -- we were not very popular at all as could be expected, imagined.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not there were any protests filed by the UN agencies?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes. I know that there had been protests made after different incidents where the UNMOs' place was shot up in East Mostar. I was myself in a convoy that went in, and we had an Armoured Personnel Carrier rolled over by accident and we were sniped at for most of an afternoon from 2.00 -- pardon me, from noon until about we were able to get out of there at around 4.30 in the afternoon. It wasn't constant but they would shoot at us. The bullets were actually hitting the overturned APC that we were hiding behind and whizzing off of it and bullets were coming close over our head. One bullet came over my left shoulder, and I saw it strike between two young boys. The bullet bounced back off the rim of the tyre and struck one of the boys in the arm actually burning and tearing and his sweater and bruising his arm. I took a photograph of that particular incident. There would be times when there would be no shooting for a while, and we would have a lot of civilians come out. At one point an older lady came out with a silver coffee service to bring us some coffee and while she was coming down a sniper started firing again and bullets were hitting all around her and she lost her coffee pot. And there was another incident of an old gentleman who had come out into the open, and he was shot at and he lost one of his shoes quickly took cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: As a result of these protests that were filed, do you know if the HVO forces took any remedial action to prevent any attacks on UNPROFOR forces or UN agencies?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I never saw any results of their actions making things better. It didn't seem to improve. However, I'm not -- I don't have knowledge of what was said to them or...

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another exhibit, please. If you could turn to 4557. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: This a document dated the 27th of August, 1993 signed by brigadier Miljenko Lasic, who was the commander of the Bosnian Croatian forces in Mostar, and it's entitled attitude towards the UN forces. And it's addressed to the HVO command with regard to the fact that members of the HVO have recently acted rationally towards the UN forces. And if you look at paragraph one, it's an order, and if you look at paragraph 1 you'll see to it, Brigadier Lasic's credit, he says all levels of command shall be obliged to undertake all measures to avoid clashes with UNPROFOR particularly, by responsible individuals and groups. Now, this appears to be a letter addressed to the HVO command in an attempt to control its forces. After the 27th of August, 1993, can you tell us whether or not there were other attacks on UNPROFOR or UN agencies?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes. That incident I just described, that was on the 7th of October, 1993. In November -- it was in November 1993 the other incident I was describing when I was sleeping in the UNMO house in East Mostar and it had been shot at all night long and the four bullets actually passed through into the room that I was in. There was another incident. I'm not really sure of the date. I think it was around the 27th of September when one of the UNMOs armoured trucks was hit by mortar and caught fire and burnt up. And there was an incident when -- when we were in East Mostar between the 22nd and 29th of August when I was -- I was hit with shrapnel from a mortar blast that straddled the APC that I was on, and there was a bullet through the bumper of the UNMOs' vehicle, one of their soft skin vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you tell us which of the protagonists forces, either the Bosnian Croats or the Bosnian Muslims, were better armed?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: The HVO were the better armed. I saw that they had tanks, heavy artillery. I witnessed some sort of rockets that they -- they would launch. People they used to call them Katyusha rockets, but I'm not sure if they were. I saw that they had big mortars, I would estimate they would probably be 88-millimetre mortars, as well as smaller mortars and on the end -- their personal weapons and small arms, I saw a Bofors gun mounted on the back of a truck at one point. It looked like a Bofors anti-aircraft gun, and I seen the results of it one time when it was fired over at a mosque in East Mostar. I -- as far as the BiH forces went I never saw anything that they had bigger than their personal rifles, and they used to make, with plastic explosives, they used to make a hand bomb that they used to throw and I believe it was made with Semtex.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, during your period -- the period of your tour within Mostar,, did you see the HVO use this heavy weaponry that you've described?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did. As I said earlier about the watching the rockets being launched and triangulating where they were being fired from, and I witnessed while in East Mostar heavy shells coming in. As a matter of fact at night when there was -- it was to dangerous to sleep on top of the cab, we used to take turns standing in the hatch and listening to the shells come in, and the bigger shells of course they would whistle before they struck. There were some on some occasion they would whistle in, and I'd duck into the APC, and then I could actually smell the smell of the explosive after it hit. With the mortars that dropped in normally, we didn't hear anything until they exploded. But it was obvious from the impact angle on the road of the smaller mortars that I saw and from the fragmentation patterns, you could tell that the mortars had been coming from the west and -- and that was the direction that they came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And -- and this shelling and mortgaging that you described, was this a sporadic or was it continuous over the period of your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: It was pretty well continuous every time I was in East Mostar. There was always small-arms fire, and there was usually always mortar or artillery or tank fire. Sometimes heavy, sometimes to a lesser degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us how often did you travel into Mostar from Medjugorje to conduct your duties?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Well, when I eventually was able to get in as I say the very first time was on the 21st of August, 1993, and then the second time I went in with the convoy was the 25th of August, and that we were detained there four days. The next -- I went on my CTO which was my accumulated leave of six days, and I had some other leave, so I was gone for a while. I came back and my next trip in was on the 13th of September. It was a very short trip in with Mr. Sorensen and three of our monitors, and it was just an introduction of those monitors to the BiH police. Then I went in a couple of days later, and the plan was I was to go in on a 24-hour rotation with the Spanish Battalion. I had to go alone because of the limited sleeping accommodations in the Armoured Personnel Carrier. Then I would be out for 48 hours and would -- would be to go back in, but this never ever occurred because when we get in there, we wouldn't be allowed to come out, or we wouldn't allowed to be in. So and then after the -- I believe it was after the 8th of October and the 11th of October because of the -- some of the statements obtained, that's when it was decided that I had to hand deliver my reports to Sarajevo. So that was taking two days of every week. So it was normally maybe once a week that I was getting into East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And how long on average of those trips did you stay over one day or --

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: On average -- on average it would be two days because there were a number of occasions it would be only one night and I would come out the next day but there were other times when I'd be in there three days, and so I would say on average two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you ever encounter hindrance when you were attempting to carry out your duties from any source?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: The only hindrance that I received was on -- when we would be going in, we were usually always stopped at a roadblock somewhere and made to wait for a number of hours and -- and then finally allowed to proceed and again on several occasions we weren't allowed to come out, or they wouldn't allow the other patrol in to relieve us so we would end up staying an extra day or two in there. As far as hindrance in East Mostar from the BiH, I was advised that they had announced over their radio that I was to be given all cooperation of any armed authority of the BiH, and I was told that I could take any photographs I wanted, photograph anything I wanted, and I was never hindered in my investigations in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, during the period you were conducting your tour of duty, was there on going fighting in the city?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, there was. The fighting was going on constantly. However, there would be -- in that period of time there would be bigger battles. For example, in September I received a request from Zagreb to try and locate 27 people who had been queried by their families and whatnot, they didn't know where they were, and I wasn't able to get in to Mostar actually until the 28th of September, eight days, because there was a very heavy shelling and fighting going on at that time in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did the fighting that took place was between the two main protagonist forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And during all of this fighting, how would the Bosnian Muslim population who were situate on the east side fare? What were the conditions for them?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Their conditions were terrible. They -- their -- I described in one of my reports and I know it -- it doesn't sound possible it sounds like an exaggeration but it wasn't. In the area that I had access to there was literally not a square metre of any building or vehicle that didn't have some sort of war scar on it, be it bullet holes, shrapnel, or fragmentation scars. The infrastructure, there was no -- no electricity. The -- there were a few generators. There was one located at the hospital. That was used sparingly to dimly light one main hallway and to light one operating room, and this hospital had apparently been the library at one time. There was a generator in the police station. Again, it didn't -- it wasn't powerful enough to provide much light there. I remember in one incident having to because of the heavy shelling we had to go down to the basement, and I had to take some statements using my little Mag light, holding it in my mouth and writing out the statements to see. The water there was not enough water to go around. At the hospital this one night I was there on the 26th of August, the hallway was covered in blood. There was blood on all of the stretchers and litters that were there. There wasn't enough water to wash it away. The smell of blood was very, very strong. It was very hot in there. And at one point I went outside to get air, and when I was out there there had been a lot of mortar shots coming in in the vicinity of where the noise of the generator was. The night was very dark, and I took some air outside in a -- laying on the floor of an ambulance that was parked behind, and I decided because of the mortars coming in I should probably go back inside. And on my way back in a mortar hit, and I was fortunate enough to be protected by the big stone stairs but some of the fragments that were fairly well spent hit me in the -- in the foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you know whether the hospital was spared from the shelling and shooting that you described earlier?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. As I say, at that particular time there was mortars falling through the night all around it. I recall on one patrol I made in there on the 4th of September that -- or pardon me on the 4th of October, the night of the 4th into the early morning of the 5th the hospital was shelled and one doctor and two other people were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: You spoke very -- a few moments ago about the water situation. Had the population of Eastern Mostar increased as a result of the conflict because of movement from west to east?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes. It was hard to judge from -- because most of the people were staying indoors away from the shelling and the sniper fire, but every morning when I would be there they used to have a water truck that would pull up and park beside the Spanish Armoured Personnel Carriers and people would begin before daylight coming to collect water from the water truck. This truck was out in the open but it was where it was located it was fairly well-protected from sniper fire and from direct artillery fire by the two big buildings and the one that our APCs were sheltering behind. However, on one occasion I remember a mortar coming in when the street was full of people to get water and it hit fortunately on the roof of the house across the street and it exploded, and all of the shrapnel and the fragmentation went up and above the people. If it had have been 30 feet short then I would assume everybody in the street probably myself would have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And was this on a once-off situation this happened --

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, I saw this happen quite often when mortars would come in. On one -- one night I was in there, I'm just trying to remember the date for sure, that would have been the night of the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: 7th of?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Of October 1993. It was -- we had got in there late, and we only had the two Armoured Personnel Carriers. That was the night -- they day that the one had rolled over, and we'd been under sniper fire all afternoon. That particular night I remember at one point there were five heavy explosions from what I assume to be mortars very, very close to us, within a hundred metres of us, and those five came in in less than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: From what you described of people queueing for the water and the mortars coming in, would it be a fair assessment to say it was a pretty risky business in queueing for that?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: It was very risky, and it was so easy for -- you know, as I say 30 feet on that one particular incident would have killed a number of people. The people were very desperate though to get water, and I recall one incident that really sticks out in my mind. I was in there and we were getting ready to leave, another platoon came in of APCs to relieve us, and as I was sitting on top of the APC, the one I was going to be going out in, a fight broke out in the line between two HVO -- pardon me, between two Muslim BiH soldiers, and one of the soldiers pulled his pistol from his holster and cocked it and put it to the head of the other soldier and that soldier, he pulled a hand grenade from his vest and pulled the pin out of the hand grenade and was hanging on to the soldier who had the gun to his head. And I saw this and I tried to settle them down and calm them down and was asking them to, you know, put their weapons away. And one of the BiH policemen who happened to be in the area, he saw it as well and he'd come and he got between them. And the man with the pistol reholstered his pistol. The other man put the pin back into the grenade, bent his pin and put it back in his vest. And the thing that really amazed me about the incident is that all of the people right beside them in line for the water, none of them moved away to lose their position in the line -- the line despite the danger of gunfire or a grenade explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Is this indicative to you of how desperate they were for the water?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, water was like gold.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And apart from water how about other commodities, flour, rice, oil were these readily available in Eastern Mostar during the period that you were touring?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, sir, they weren't. And when the first time I went in there, I really saw that the people -- they basically looked like they were starving, starving to death slowly. And after UNHCR convoys started coming, in the situation became a little bitter but at no time did I ever see any food for sale in any kind of a shop or market or anything like that. I believe the only way that they would get it would be meted out by the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And given the desperate situation that the Bosnian Muslim population found themselves in, what was the situation in Mostar from July through to August from 1993 specifically on the movement of -- of convoys and the movement of humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: In -- in July there were no convoys of food or humanitarian aid getting into Mostar at all that I was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: They had been -- they wouldn't let the convoys go in the HVO wouldn't let any convoys into Mostar at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: How are you aware of that? Are you aware from personal knowledge or reports?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, I was stationed there and at that time we would be trying to get in ourselves, and we would always be turned back at the check-points. And it was the same thing for UNHCR and all of the other agencies. We used to generally on Monday mornings have a meeting of all the agencies and that meeting would be held at the Spanish battalion's headquarters in Medjugorje, and there would be representatives of each of the United Nations organisations and the International Red Cross, and they would all give a brief report on any progress they made and at that time no one was being allowed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, I think you said that a relief column did get through in August 1993?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, the very first one that went in was on the 21st of August, that was a Saturday, and it was primarily medical supplies. One of the -- there was a so-called cease-fire in effect, and - however there was still sniper fire coming in from the west side - we were able to take one of the APCs that was filled with the medical supplies to the hospital old library, park in the back there and unload it. And then we had to walk alongside of the -- the APC on the sheltered side of it to get back across this one particular sniper area to -- where the rest of the APCs were.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And how long did that -- how long did that convoy remain in the city, and was it able to leave safely?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, it was able to leave safely. We were only in there I would say about three on a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And in relation to another convoy you were present with the convoy that was held up in the city?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct. The very next convoy to go in left on the 25th of August. It was supposed to leave in the morning. However, it was held up held -- held up and we were still negotiating getting it in. And we were finally able to leave the Spanish Battalion camp in Medjugorje, and we went as far as Citluk. And at Citluk there was a demonstration going on by the civilians there, and the road was blocked. And we were held up there for a further -- about a further six hours I guess. And then we were finally allowed to proceed, and we made it as far as the airport. And at the airport we were -- we conducted a body exchange, and during this whole time that this body exchange was going on it was -- it started at approximately 2200 or 10.00 p.m.. There was still fighting going on there was -- we could see tracer bullets going over top of us fairly high up, and we were seeing explosions hitting on the -- on the BiH side. There was a fire, I recall, up on the hill from the explosions, and of course the smell was terrible because the bodies on both sides, a lot of them had been buried for a number of months and were dug up to be exchanged, and we were finally allowed to proceed in. And it was well after midnight that we got into East Mostar, and we -- myself and Mr. Sorensen, we tried to meet up with the BiH police to re-establish contact for CIVPOL, and we did this. We had a meeting. And with Mr. Salko Zuljevic, and then we were getting to get ready to get back on the APCs to leave, and we were told that the civilian population of Mostar weren't going to let us leave and they'd at first -- first sign of it was that they wouldn't unload the last truck, and then finally a truck was pulled across and blocked the exit for the convoy, and then a bus was pulled in the middle of the convoy effectively dividing it into two sections.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And could you tell us why -- why ultimately you learned that you couldn't leave?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, from my talks and Mr. Sorensen's talks with Mr. Zuljevic we, learned that the HVO had just completed an offensive and had taken the dam and they had controlled the water level and raised the water level cutting off some of the supply crossings that the BiH had to supply their small pockets on the west side of the Neretva River and that they feared an all-out attack that would come and wipe out the population on the east side, and so they were wanting to keep the United Nations people there and the world press that was there with us at the time as protection against that happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Ultimately did you -- was the release of the convoy negotiated and did you leave safely?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir. After -- on the fourth day we were able to negotiate a release, myself and Mr. Sorensen took an active part in those negotiations. And in the end I was able to get the driver of the truck that the bus had been removed earlier, so we were able to get the convoy into one unit again, and then I -- I directed traffic out through a sniper started shooting at that point and some of the trucks stopped. So Mr. Sorensen had to run ahead and keep them going, and I directed traffic until the last truck that was going through, and I stopped it and jumped in with a couple of British drivers, and we left East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you know from where the sniper fire was coming at the time?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It was coming from over on the west side of Mostar in the HVO controlled area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
