utterances.text: And was it being directed at any ABiH military positions that you could see?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No BiH military positions that I could see. It was being directed at the UNHCR trucks as they were coming through openings where there was an angle of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I have a number of exhibits that I wish to put to the witness, Your Honour, but perhaps now might be a good time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we will have a break now and we will resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We resume our session.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Mr. Forbes, just before I deal with some exhibits, could I just ask you, during the currency of your tour, was there a defined confrontation line between the protagonist forces in Mostar that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, there was. It might shift a little teeny bit from time to time but there was a line.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell us that line was it situate on the west bank or the east bank of the river?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: It was on the west bank of the river as the high BiH held a little bit of territory on the west side of the Neretva that I was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And the area on the east bank occupied by most of the Bosnian Muslim population, were there any large concentration of ABiH troops that you saw in those buildings?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I never saw any barracks or any large number of BiH troops at any time. About the most I would see would probably be maybe 20 soldiers going along the street at one time going either north or south past our positions and 20 would probably be the -- by far the most I'd ever seen together at one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to go back to exhibit 5009 if you would for me. You looked at it earlier.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And you described this. This is the incident report that -- the example that you gave to Their Honours of what the incident report looked like and you described the first page. Could you turn over to the second page, please, where it says form 2.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And you have a number of boxes and you have two -- the first two boxes are filled in?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And this appears to be basically an expansion of your report as to what you did on that occasion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct. It -- the top box as it says on there the complaint/witness explanation, and the second block is the description of the scene of the action or the scene of the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And on that occasion if we look at the first box briefly it appears that you introduced two new monitors to the BiH police, and on that occasion you were being established as the liaison between BiH and CIVPOL; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct, only there were three new monitors being introduced to them at that time. There was Frederick Garcia who is a gendarmerie from France, Constable Jancewicz who is a Canadian, and Mr. Jodlowski who was from Poland.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And second paragraph in the first box, the second last line says: "Small-arms fire is constant and mortars land at very frequent intervals." Was that something that you saw yourself or were told -- was told?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, I saw that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Indeed. And if we look at the second box it says: "East Mostar has been very badly shelled, and there is hardly a building or vehicle that has not been damaged to some extent." Again, was that something that you personally observed or were told by the officials who you met with BiH police?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's something that I personally observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And these buildings which had been badly damaged and shelled, this goes back to my earlier question whether the ABiH forces occupied these buildings.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No. There were not military personnel in those vehicles or -- pardon me, in those buildings that I was aware of. These buildings were just -- a lot of them had been stores or private homes, but there were no military buildings that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Is there any reason --

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: There was one building that I understood had been a military headquarters that had been blown up, but I'd never seen troops in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So these buildings which you saw, is there any particular reason that you know of or were informed of that they should be targeted by the opposing forces?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Not legitimately, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: If you turn over to the third page, you have a notation there in the centre of the page, the 16th of September, 1993. Did you return again on the 16th of September, 1993, to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went back in with the Spanish Battalion's patrol, and I was the only CIVPOL monitor at that time going in.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And on that occasion, or if we look at the last paragraph, there's reference to heavy shelling that occurs about every night, and it says: "It was learned that two days previous to this date the shelling had been particularly heavy. Rockets, heavy artillery, large-calibre mortars, and tank cannons had laid down a very heavy barrage." Is that what you were told?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, and I could see a lot of new damage as well, but from interviewing civilians through my interpreter and through interviews with the BiH police, I was told that -- and also from the UN UNMOs that told me as well, and they were there during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Your report on the next page page 4 at the top it says: "It was reported that several were killed and wounded." Did you see any of these people? Did you witness the bodies or did you visit any of the wounded to be able to verify that had been killed -- people killed or wounded?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Just down -- it would be one, two -- about four to five blocks down further south from where we parked was a mosque that the space in front of it had been -- was being used as a graveyard, and it was always -- there was always open graves there being filled on a daily basis, and the -- I observed the wooden markers on the graves, and I could see from the dates on there that it was an ongoing thing, that people were dying every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you know whether or not those people who were buried, whether they had died from natural causes or as a result of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Most of the people and the names, I also noted that their ages were very young, and it would be highly unlikely that that many young people would be dying of natural causes and I just assumed that it was from the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, just looking at page 4 again in the second paragraph, during this visit is it correct that during the time of your visit you were present during shelling?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct. It was considered to be moderate to light by Mostar standards, and it was usually around three heavy shells an hour were landing at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: On that occasion did you receive information from UNMOs with regard to further population displacement from the west to the east?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, they advised that people were still being forced across -- across the line from west over to East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did they indicate when this had taken place and the manner in which it had taken place?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: They were -- it always happened at night in the dark, and it was an ongoing thing. It was almost a nightly occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, would you look now, please, to the next exhibit in your bundle, which is Exhibit 5215.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I have it here, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: If we look at the front page again, this is an incident report, and it's dated the 20th of September, and it's on the right-hand side, a CIVPOL name Larry Forbes. Is this a report prepared by you?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, this is one of my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if we look down at the bottom of the front page it has a brief summary and largely this refers to a request for tracing and results of tracing, tracing of missing persons?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if we open the second page, you will see at the top that there's a date, the 1st to the 10th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The reason that the original date on there is the 20th, that would have been the date that the requests -- we received the requests from Zagreb to do this tracing, but because of the heavy fighting I was unable to get in there until the 28th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if we look in second page which is marked form 3, the first paragraph, it says halfway down the paragraph: "It was impossible to get into East Mostar due to the extremely savage shelling that took place there last week. At times there were up it a thousand heavy shells an hour falling in Mostar." Was this information reported to you?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: From who?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: From the United Nations UNMO personnel who were in the city, in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if we look then at the next exhibit which is 5539?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, I have it sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Is this another incident report?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And again in fact this is dated the 1st to the 10th, 1993, also.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And is this a more expanded version of your report relating back to the tracing --

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: -- request?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, it is and also what else had taken place during that particular patrol into East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And looking at the first page last line it says: "From the last visit by CIVPOL, it was felt that things could not get worse than they already were. This was a false assumption. However, things -- however, because things in fact were worse. In the last week East Mostar has undergone an extremely heavy shelling by artillery, heavy mortars, and tank cannons. UNMOs advised at least 20 heavy impacts a minute were hitting East" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you kindly read more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: This is related to the last report that you mentioned; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned at an earlier stage that the position with regard to water and what people had to do for water, if we look at third paragraph on page seven of this report. It says it begins with the people begin to line up for the water truck which comes to the location beside the Spanish APC vehicles very early in the morning. Is this to what you were referring to earlier when you gave evidence that people were queueing up for water?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn, slow.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And halfway down the paragraph it says: "Everyone, young and old alike, are forced to run across this area with every chance of being shot. This is only one of several areas that are exposed to sniper fire during this visit."

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I thought you had indicated earlier that there were tall buildings that protected where the truck was parked.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: There were. However, about a hundred feet further -- no, not a hundred feet. About a hundred metres further north of where the truck would be parked, there was an opening where there was a line of fire and it was subject to sniper fire when people would cross that particular opening. Sometimes the line would be so long that some people would be actually on the other side of that sniper opening, and they would wait until there was room and then dash across and then be on the line on the safe side of it further south to get the water from the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And you mentioned the delivery of the water in the morning. Was this once-off delivery every day or a number of times during the day to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: It used to come once a day that I was aware of, early in the morning as I say, and people would start queueing up before daylight.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And was there sufficient water to go around for all of the population?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: The people that would come, they would usually have containers maybe about a maximum of 10 gallons, possibly as high as 15 gallons per person, and that would have to do them the day for their drinking, washing, cooking, whatever they were using. It was not really adequate for the people's needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the next exhibit, please. It's Exhibit number 5625. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And again is this an incident report dated the 6th of October, 1993, and was it prepared by you?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if we turn to the second page, the second box. You say that on that date East Mostar was still controlled by the BiH forces. It has been the scene of very heavy shelling. On each visit, more and more war damage is evident. There is not a building or a vehicle in the area of the city that Monitor Forbes has been able to patrol that has not been hit --

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: -- by shell fragments or bullets."

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: If we turn then to page 6 of that report.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: There's reference made to a visit that you took. Did you take the opportunity on that occasion to visit, to see the conditions that people were living in?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did. I visited some of the basements where the people were living. Just about everybody that could find space was living underground at this particular time because it was dangerous to be living above ground with the shelling. And I visited some basements of big old concrete and stone buildings. Would you like me to describe --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: The -- the basements were generally concrete floors, concrete walls. People were living in mattresses -- on mattresses, on the floors. It was quite crowded this these places. There was no electricity or running water or bathroom facilities that I could see. They were lit in most instances by candlelight. In some of the buildings I was in, they had made little stalls like vegetable-type bins and a family would have one of these stalls and sometimes they would hang a blanket to give a little more privacy and whatnot for their family, but they were very crowded and it was very dirty and dusty down in there. And as I say, no, no real amenities that I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Why was there not the electricity available to the population?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Because of the war situation and the HVO controlled the power in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did people venture out in public during the days that -- during the day that you saw? Would you see a lot of people strolling on the streets?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, not very often. I would just see people on the streets in the day time other than when they would be lining up for the truck to get their water. It was quite dangerous to just walk around outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So where would most people spend their time?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I assume that they were all inside either in the basements or inside other shelters. The one exception was we used to get a lot of the little kids would come and climb on the Spanish APCs and play around there, and it was considered dangerous situation, and the BiH police as well as the Spanish soldiers did their best to discourage this and keep them away.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, you have referred on -- on a number of occasions during your testimony today to either -- either reports received from others, UNMO, BiH otherwise as to forced transfers of Bosnian Muslims from west side to the east side. Did it occur, did it happen that you conducted interviews with individuals who claimed to have been forcibly removed from their homes on the west side to the east side?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I recall on the 8th of October, 1993, two Jordanian UNMOs and their interpreter picked me up at the Spanish APCs and we went to a building that had apparently had been a department store before the war, and up on the second floor it was a big sturdy stone and concrete building and in a big open room on the third floor there was 34 people who had been forced across the -- the line in the night -- the night before, and a couple previous nights as well. Thirty-four were there at that particular time. There were some mattresses on the floor that they could sleep on. There were three or four chairs, as I remember, and maybe one or two tables and other than that there was no other -- no other furniture there was no toilet facilities that I could see there, no -- again no running water or electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you conduct on that occasion an interview of Bosnian Muslims who had come from the west to the east?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I don't want you to mention any names for the moment, please.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So you did conduct an interview on that occasion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I actually took a statement from three people, and then I had to leave because the UNMOs' interpreter had to leave and because of the situation I had to go with them to back to the Spanish parking area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I'd like to refer you to -- but before I -- to one of your exhibits, but before I do I think, I should apply to go into private session here, Your Honours, because these exhibits not only the refer to expulsions but there's also reference to assaults of a delicate nature, a sexual nature, on a number of females, and their names are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. By this time there was a -- Mr. Cedric Thornberry and a number of higher up United Nations authorities had arrived in Medjugorje, and we also had a young United Nations press officer or reporter by the name of David Belham from New Zealand, who was very concerned about the situation too, and he was doing everything he could to help us resolve it. And we had approached Mr. Thornberry trying to stress the seriousness of the situation and to get some sort of help in resolving this that he was -- they -- he told us that they had a plan that they were going to try and get a convoy in, and this was the results of that was finally the convoy that went in on the 21st of August. The situation did eventually resolve itself in that the men were released from the Heliodrom, and they had to sell off all of their property at rock-bottom prices, but at least the families were allowed to leave as families and they were -- all left for different places. I'm not sure exactly where they all ended up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: In relation to this incident did you meet anybody within the HVO military to discuss the matter with them?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: There was one -- one day myself and Leo Sorensen we continued on the road past Ljubuski, and it follows -- I remember quite well it follows a valley, and up this valley we had -- I believe as one HVO policemen had mentioned who we had been talking to, and he had some English, he had mentioned that there was a general staying along the road. So we ended up tracking this person down, and he seemed to be shocked that we actually found him, and he was -- I don't remember his rank insignia, but I do remember that he was treated with great deference by the other soldiers who were nearby and by that one police officer. We explained as best we could, I believe he had some English, and we were able to explain that was going on. He appeared to play -- pay lip-service to us, and we did tell him about this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you remember what that officer looked like?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I remember he was a big man. I remember he had a full head of silvery grey hair. I would say that he was approximately 5, 10 to 5, 11 inches in height.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did he have any other distinctive features such as mole on his check, a moustache such as you're carrying?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I'm sorry sir, I can't honestly say that I remember this long that far back, a real good description of his face.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you know the name of this general?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you know at the time?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I heard that it started with P, but I don't know what the name was. I used to have problems with pronunciation and spelling of the names, and I couldn't say for certain what his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And this brings me almost to the end of the -- of your testimony. How long did you stay in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I stayed there until the end of November into early December and we were -- we went out to leave. We had the -- a medal parade in Croatia, but then our -- our mandate -- our mission got extended one week, so I went back to Mostar. And when they found out I was coming back, I was told that they wanted me to come in and it was sort of like a little surprise party, but they had to let me know that it was going on, and I was able to get into East Mostar one more time, and this time I went in in a soft-skinned vehicle with a new Spanish soldier to the area who didn't realise the danger. And a lot of -- he didn't speak English, and he didn't speak Serbo-Croatian. A lot of the people were yelling at him that he's going to get shot any minute, and I was trying to explain this to him too, but we eventually made it to the UNMOs house. From there I went and attended a farewell gathering in the police station. There was myself, chief Maslesa, deputy chief Zuljevic, Mr. Sejic, the chief of the detectives, and there was one other police officer who had been on courses with the RCMP in Canada at one time, and they gave me a drawing the Stari Mostar bridge and a few little mementos. After that I went back up to the UNMOs house, and I must I have to admit that at this time there was a bit of a battle going on, because there were shells falling in the East Mostar area at the time, and I'd have to at times run across open areas. And I finally went back. And then I went with a couple of Jordanian UNMOs, we were going to supervise an air drop of food packets from American C 130 Hercules, and the packets -- it was supposed to be secret, were going to be dropped higher up on the mountain because an earlier air drop of food packets, the people had been hit by mortars and machine-gun fire while they were gathering up the food. So this was higher up the mountain, and I remember as we climbed up there I would run into people on the mountain, mainly older people. And I remember running into a couple of men were just in their undershorts and jackets, they had taken their jeans and they had tied the legs together and stuffed the pants with food packets extra food packets, and they were sort of carrying them like horse collars over around their neck. And I supervised that, well, as the best we could up in the dark there, and I remember too that at that time there was a four-gun emplacement over on Mount Hum with of 155-millimetre guns, I recall that's what they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Who occupied Mount Hum at the time?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Mount Hum was occupied by the HVO. And I remember at one point the whole top of the mountain lit up as if a brilliant flash of lightning, but there was no sound of course. And then about seven seconds later we are could hear the heavy shells whistling in, and they exploded with tremendous force down in the valley below us. And then I finally left in the morning from the UNMO residence, and as I was leaving it was getting on going on to daylight there was fires burning from the fighting the night before and that was my last view of East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And at the time you were leaving, end of November start of December, did you notice any reduction in the spate of shelling and shooting that was coming from the western side to the eastern side?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: It seemed to go in spurts. There would be times when the shelling would be very, very heavy and it would appear like -- and then there would be a bit of a respite as if they had to resupply because they would be low on -- on heavy shells and explosives. And so after a period of very heavy shelling, there would usually be a respite where the -- the firing of heavy guns and mortars would be light to moderate by Mostar standards. But at the end that particular night when I left it was as bad as ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And the deportations or the transport -- the deportations of people from the western side to the eastern side that you have described and reports that you received of it, did you continue to receive reports of this up to the time that you departed, or was there a period that they ceased?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, basically up to the time I departed this practice had still been going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you know from the reports that received, do you know what happened to the accommodations and property of the Bosnian Muslims that came from the west to the east?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't know what became of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: At this stage I don't have any further questions, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Forbes, as far as I'm concerned, I would have some questions I would like to put to you in line with -- in the same line as the questions that have been put to you by the Prosecution. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My first question: You said at a certain time that on this line, the separation line between the front, you had seen about some 20 soldiers from the BiH soldiers, and I was quite surprised to hear that because when there's a separation line you may think that there are forces on both sides of the line in quite a great number, but here it seems that you said that you have seen some 20 soldiers. Did I misunderstand what you said, or could you say that more clearly?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Those 20 soldiers that I saw were actually in -- on the street I believe it's called Malesa Tita street, where we used to park the APCs, and that was the most soldiers I saw at any one time on that particular street. As far as the soldiers who were actually on the confrontation line, when we would cross over the line we always battened down the hatches in the APCs, so I really didn't have a chance to see the soldiers on either side right at the front line, and where we were -- where we were parked and where and I operated to go to the police station and whatnot, I didn't actually have a direct view of the line of confrontation. So I can't say how many soldiers on either side of that line there were, and the soldiers that I were referring to at the time I saw maybe 20 at the most, they were just going -- it looked like a line of maybe miners on their way to work at the mine just walking up the street, and they were going north at that time on Tito street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this element of precision. One more question: When you were in East Mostar during the -- the time you carried out your responsibilities in the frame of your mission, were you able to see by yourself the fact that the people living in East Mostar were somehow not in the possibility of leaving East Mostar because of the presence of HVO, or do you believe that the inhabitants of the East Mostar -- do you believe they would have been able to leave the area if they wanted to? What is your own feeling on the freedom of movement of people living in the east part of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. They weren't able to leave. They weren't allowed to leave and go back across the HVO lines. As a matter of fact, I had one incident. There was a lady whose name was Sana, and she was born in Italy originally, and she was, I believe, a fairly wealthy lady at one time and she seemed to be a very classy person. Her husband who was sick, and as a result he couldn't fight for the BiH, and she lived there with her husband and her grandfather. And in order to be of use and to be able to get a better ration, she had been acting as an interpreter. And the way I understood, it at first she was an interpreter for the BiH military but she also did some interpreting for us on the first -- on the incident when the whole convoy was held up. She had -- I got to know her a little bit, and she had asked me if it would be possible that I might be able to send a letter for her to Italy so that they could send her Italian documentation and that she may be able then to arrange passage out of Bosnia to Italy, and I did this when I was on my -- on my cumulated leave. I sent the message for her, and she did in fact receive her documents, and the BiH allowed her and her husband and her grandmother to leave. And that was on the trip -- the trip of the 28th, 29th, and I guess it would have been on the 30th of -- of September that we were coming out, and she and her husband and grandmother were in the ambulance APC. Just to explain, Your Honour, our patrol, there were six Armoured Personnel Carriers, four normal ones, the ambulance APC was fifth in the line, and then the command APC with the lieutenant and the one I travelled in was sixth in line. So we ended up leaving, and we were heading out and we got to the first check-point in HVO territory on the east side of the Neretva River north of where the American bridge was located. It would be in the Buna area, south of the Buna area, and the first four Armoured Personnel Carriers of our patrol were allowed to proceed and they stopped the last two, the ambulance one and the one that I was in, and the HVO were demanding that the APC be opened so that they could search it, and we were refusing to do that. And after a period of time we were held there, they had placed anti-vehicle mines across the front of the road in front of our two APCs with dowelling in them which controlled a trip mechanism on the top, so that if you tried to pass by, you hit the dowelling and that would trigger the mine. Eventually through negotiation we were eventually allowed to proceed, and we did proceed. And to make a long story short, we ended up getting back into Medjugorje, and her and her husband and grandmother were eventually allowed to go back to Italy. But the word got around that I had helped arrange for someone to get out, and a lot of people used to come to the APCs where I was -- at night where I was, and request -- and you know there was nothing I could do to help them, and they weren't allowed to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From your answer it seems that the HVO from the check-points was able to check the movements of the people, but how can you then explain that at a certain time you said that the BiH could be supplied using mules. You said that at the beginning of this morning's session. Was there a possibility for East Mostar to be supplied through passages where HVO did not have any check-points?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: As I say, I never personally saw this path, but I was led to believe that a small amount of -- of supplies were able to get through the mountains, but it was my understanding that this was very, very difficult terrain and very difficult to go anywhere that way, and it was basically going north towards Sarajevo. And I personally never did see that trail, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question has to do with a document which I would like you to have a look at 553 -- 5539. This is a report made by you, and please look at the second page of this report, and also I'm telling the Prosecution that the second page apparently has a number 7. Obviously some pages are missing in this document, but I just want to ask questions about page 7. And, Mr. Forbes, please look at the third paragraph of page 7 where you speak about the water, the truck, the people who are coming to get water from the truck, and I can read that you say that there is an open area where snipers on the HVO side can see the street. Now, this sentence caused me to ponder, because according to what one could understand in your report, you were on the premises yourself. So could you confirm that what you describe here, you have saw it with your own eyes.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did see it with my own eyes. Once I would get back to the APCs after my meetings and work and in the evening when it was starting to get dark there was nowhere that you could basically go, so I used to sit up on top of the Armoured Personnel Carrier and watch what was going on. And I used to watch the different methods that people use running across. Some would crouch down and make themselves as small as possible, others would run stand straight and run, and some would run in a zigzag pattern, and on several occasions I saw near misses where these people would be fired at, and it didn't make any difference if they were women, men, or children, they would all be fired at. There was only one person that I recall that used to walk, it was an old lady who everybody said was crazy, and she used to walk back and forth across that opening and they didn't shoot at her. And it almost seemed like she was trying to commit suicide, but they didn't shoot her. But everybody else were taking their own lives in their hands when they -- when they crossed that open area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I am interested in is what you say concerning the fact that snipers were in the HVO area. What enables you to say so?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: The angle of fire that was coming -- where the bullets were coming down and the angle that they were hitting the street. They were coming from the west and the higher ground over on the west or the higher buildings on the west which were HVO-controlled areas. The people that were being shot at, some of the men that were going across were BiH military who would be off duty and walking down the street and the same with the civilians. They were all Muslim civilians, and I'm sure that the HVO wouldn't be shooting at their own soldier -- I mean the BiH wouldn't be shooting at their own soldiers or their own women and children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You indicate, on line 13 of page 89, that this came from higher-up buildings. You noticed that there were buildings which had a certain height.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I didn't do -- spend much time, sir, actually looking around the corner but, yeah, from where the -- the way this opening was, it was a line of fire or an alley of fire that came from the west side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you are affirmative on this? You confirm that there is no ambiguity?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I'm sure of that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will ask my colleagues if they have any questions for the witness. Right. We said that we would stop the hearing at 1.00, so perhaps we'd better pause now, have a break now so that everybody can rest, and we will resume at a quarter past 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.38

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I believe is somebody from the Defence wants to intervene. Is that you, Mr. Murphy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. May we go into private is session for just one or two moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Regarding the time granted to the Defence, the Prosecution did not use three hours as scheduled but only two hours and 22 minutes; therefore, the Defence will have three hours. Each counsel may have 30 minutes according to -- or depending on changes. Who wants to start? Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'm going to begin first. Since I have been given some time from Mr. Pusic's Defence, I think that I will need time until 3.00 or five past 3.00, maybe 10 minutes exceeding my time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Witness, good afternoon. I'm addressing the witness. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I please ask the usher, before we begin, if we can be efficient and if he can give the witness the binder that I will be using, and all the others in the courtroom have received that binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to begin with your mission's report under number 503415. It's a report on the death of Lieutenant Francisco. It's a report, as we can see on the last page, dated the 13th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Ma'am, what was the number again, 5039?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I have found it, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: At the beginning, there is no date, so could you please confirm that on the last page near the signature there is that date? Can you just confirm that this report is of the 13th of July, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said that you typed this report?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You also said you partly participated in the investigation or rather, that you were present when members of the Spanish Bat were questioned. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. I was, as I say, after most of the investigation was over, some of the Spanish soldiers that had been involved I'd heard what they had to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, also confirm, that you know that a post-mortem was carried out and that you had information about that at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I was informed, yes, that the post-mortem had been carried out. I had no direct knowledge or hadn't attended the post-mortem or anything of that nature, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Also, you said today that an analysis of the flak jacket was carried out of the one that the late Lieutenant Fernandez was wearing. Did you have information about that at the time the investigation was being carried out?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes. Just what I was told about it. I didn't have first-hand knowledge of it, just what I'd been told about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We heard today that the attachments that are mentioned in the report, the photo documentation; and by the last page, I think that there was some five attachments. At the time when the report was drafted, did you see those attachments, and perhaps did you see them at any point later?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I -- I remember being shown some photographs by Leo Sorensen.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: According to your information, sir, was this the final report about the death of Lieutenant Aguilar that was drafted by the UN civilian police?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I believe, yes, this was the final report. I know that -- or I believe that it was the final report that came from our station, Mostar station out of Medjugorje, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: At the time when you questioned the witnesses, when you directly took part in the drafting of that report by typing it and looking at the photographs, can we agree that the report does not definitely establish where the bullet was fired from, the bullet that struck Lieutenant Fernandez?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes. We -- it couldn't be determined to the exact foot or anything like that. It was just determined what area it came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now you are telling us that the report did establish, beyond dispute, that it came from a specific area of the town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes. I felt that it was beyond dispute. The -- the exact location of the APC, when he was hit, could not be determined, other than within a few yards in a straight line, because the way it was determined where he was, when the driver of the Armoured Personnel Carrier looked back, he was standing, and then when he looked back he was drive; and before he was to make the left-hand turn, he looked back once again, and the lieutenant was hit and had fallen down into the APC. So we knew that it had to happen in a certain -- a certain stretch; but exactly where in that stretch, it couldn't be determined.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I would like to ask you now to look at exhibit in the pink binder that you have in front of you. It's the third exhibit from the back numbered 2D 00117. You can just tell me when you've found the document?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I've found it, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I assume that you did not see this document before, but there is some information in the document that you could possibly confirm, so I would like to ask you to look at the document section by section. You also said that you know that a committee was put together by members of the HVO and members of the Spanish Battalion that was supposed to investigate and establish who was responsible for the death of Lieutenant Aguilar. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In the first paragraph, it says -- well, the document is dated the 14th of June, 1993; and in the first paragraph, it says that a meeting was held, attended by the head of defence department, Mr. Stojic; head of defence department assistant, Ivica Lucic; and chief of the military police, Valentin Coric; together with the representatives of the Spanish Battalion of the UNPROFOR. They were also joined by Colonel Castro and Major De Salas, and it was agreed for the -- Mr. De Salas to go to the Dracevo military base, where they would establish facts necessary to solve the case of Lieutenant Fernandez's death, and then it says what was established in here. The first paragraph speaks about the bullets coming from the left side under a certain angle. Do you recall that you, in the report that you typed out or during the investigations and interrogations of certain witness, you also reached the conclusion that the bullet came or the damage to the vehicle occurred on the left side?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, I didn't have knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In your report that we looked at before, the same thing is stated, but never mind. We will continue. Did you know that Captain Alvarez found a steel bullet mass, and there was an analysis carried out of the type of bullets that were fired?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I heard that there had been, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. In the next paragraph, the post-mortem is mentioned, which you said you were aware had been carried out but that you did not take part in it, and certain details were mentioned that were established during the post-mortem. I would like to draw your attention to this sentence towards the end of the passage which says: "Taking into consideration the height of the vehicle, taking into account the height -- the path of the bullet through the body, it is determined that the bullet is fired from the height of a two-storey building, taking into consideration the height of the vehicle, in which Captain Fernandez was standing on the floor and leaning to the left side." So did you reach any conclusions about the position in which Captain Fernandez was standing, and what would be the possible location or the building from which the bullet could have been fired which killed Captain Fernandez?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: From the information I was given - and, again, I didn't have this first-hand; I didn't actually do this part of the investigation myself - but the information that I had from the CIVPOL investigators, and from how the lieutenant was standing in the APC, I felt that the bullet had to come from a higher angle than a two-storey building, and that I witnessed how the crew commanders normally stood when they were squatting or bent over to look through the gap in the sandbag shield that they built on top of the Armoured Personnel Carriers. So I don't actually agree with this that it came from only a two-storey height.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. That is your opinion. Can we move to the next paragraph, please, and that is the conclusion in this report about the position or the building from which it -- the bullet was possibly fired. The passage says: "On the basis of statements from the HVO commander and HVO soldiers at the bank and gymnasium positions, we determined that none of them were in the -- were at the advance positions at the given time, and that none fired at that time. So based on expert analysis of the calibre and type of the weapon, we determined that they could not produce the mentioned effects with the weapons that they had. "Finally, from the bank and the gymnasium 's most advanced positions, there is that optical visibility of the scene of the event which we also documented with photo and video records, which we submitted for review to Spanish Bat representative, Major De Salas, and UNPROFOR civilian police representative, Mr. Sorensen." My question is: If you know that this is what happened, that Mr. Sorensen received certain video and photo material made by representatives of the HVO in this investigation, which they conducted together with members of the Spanish Battalion?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: And the question -- I'm sorry, ma'am, the question was?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The question is: If you know if Mr. Sorensen received this material from HVO representatives as it is stated in this report? This would be the photographic material of what was seen from the two positions from the building and certain video footage about the incident.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes. I can't say that I knew that. It's 14 years ago, and I don't recall ever actually seeing this report or actually ever hearing from the HVO what type of weapon it was that he was shot with, other than it being a high-powered rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, we probably didn't understand one another. I would like to go back to the photographs. In the report, it says that the most prominent positions of the bank and the gymnasium - these are two buildings that were mentioned in your report, as well as possible places of the source of the fire - so this report mentions that there is no optical visibility of the place of the incident from those two buildings, that this was photographed, and that those photographs and video footage were handed over to Mr. De Salas, who is a member of the Spanish Battalion, and Mr. -- representative of the civilian police, Mr. Sorensen. I'm just asking you if you know if such photographs were made and handed over to Mr. Sorensen.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I don't know for sure, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, do you know or can you tell the Court the following: The photographs you did see, when you were drafting the report, you said you saw certain photographs. Can you establish the source of the photographs that are mentioned in your report of the 13th of July? Are those the photographs that were actually taken by the HVO and handed over to the civilian police for -- to use them as in their investigation? Do you know the source of the photographs that you saw?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, I want to say we don't have the photographs because the Prosecutor said during the examination-in-chief that he does not have the documentation that was actually attached to the report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, ma'am. I'm not sure what the source of those photographs were or who had taken them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. It's mentioned in the report, but I don't think that you are in a position to confirm that, but here it says that: "Major De Salas, with our operatives, visited our most advanced positions. He climbed to the places where our soldiers are never positioned, because it is too dangerous. He made video recordings, and he made sure there is no possibility of shooting from these positions." Can we agree, in the report, you don't have to know that that the HVO in this report cited that you could only fire at colonel -- Lieutenant Fernandez from the east side, or rather, from the side of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It says, at the end, something about a topic that I don't wish to dwell for a long time with you, and it has to do with the accusations posed by the Spanish Minister. And, at the end, I would like to ask you to look at the last sentence of this report, which says: "The case is quite clear. As far as we are concerned, we are convinced that the death of Lieutenant Fernandez is being manipulated with, and that the UNPROFOR civilian and military police, with our assistance and the assistance of the department of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the HVO, have reconstructed the events and will give their final decision." Sir, this report that we have just read is dated of the 14th of -- of June 1993, and you have said that your final report was dated the 13th of July of 1993. Then it is obvious that in the meantime this investigation was carried out. Can you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: It would appear so. Like I say, I -- I cannot comment. I don't agree with this result, but I must -- to be fair to everybody, I'm only basing it on the information that I learned from Mr. Sorensen and the -- the Spanish soldiers that had described how the lieutenant was standing. To be very fair, you know, I cannot really be the one to dispute any of this, and it would -- would take somebody who would be more involved in the investigation to really fairly comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you for this suggestion, sir, but you're a witness and these questions were put to you by the Prosecution, so I would like to see, through you, what you can help us with and what you know. Now, could you please look in my binder of documents, 2D 00118.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is the second document from the back. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I -- yes, I have, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please look at this document. Just look at it briefly, and can you please tell me if you are familiar with this document. Did you see it? This is document. I, for the transcript and because of you, would like to stress that the document has the same date as the report that was marked P 03415, which you described as the final report on the death of Lieutenant Aguilar Fernandez Francisco. Can you please tell me if this letter is known to you, if you're familiar with this report. It's very brief, and I would just like to ask you to look at the document, to acquaint yourself with it.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I'll just read it over quickly here. Yes, ma'am, I've read it over. And you were wondering if I was familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That's correct. That was the first question.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I -- I don't remember this. Reading through it, I can see that, at that particular time, Mr. Sorensen would have been correct in that we couldn't get in to meet with the chief of police, Maslesa, in East Mostar to carry out inquiries. So I would agree this is probably right, but I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir. Sir, let's take this step-by-step. We'll get there. My question now is as follows -- the first question is: Are you familiar with this report? Have you already seen it? Did you see it on the day that it was drafted or at any subsequent point in time?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I may have, but I don't -- I don't remember it. The other report, when I glanced at it, I remembered it right off the bat. I'll explain one of the reasons I remembered it. The city in Canada that I come from, the daily paper is known as "The Gleaner," and I started using that word in reports as a young constable. Reading it over, I noticed my use of the word in there, and I remembered that report. But in all fairness, I can't say that, after 14 years, that I do remember this -- this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you confirm that this is Mr. Sorensen's signature on the report?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I couldn't now. No. I can't remember his signature that well after all these years. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's have a look at a report again, since you have said that you can't remember it. Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOVICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document I'm interested in is P 03415. I'd like to have a look at the last page of that document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I could just take a second to glance at some of the other reports I have that Mr. Sorensen has signed, I could -- I could compare them to see if they look similar and that than might be helpful. Would that be all right?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOVICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. Thank you. That's why I asked you to have a look at P 03415. That's the report that you typed out, a report that we had a look at a minute ago. 3415. Let's have a look at the last page. You have two separate binders, and it's very easy to compare the signatures.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, they certainly look to be the same. I would -- I would say yes that's -- that's his signature. The same as the one on this report. So I'm not being an expert in handwriting, but that certainly looks like that to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to identify the document, you can see that it says "Memo" at the top, "UNCIVPOL Memo," and you can see the date. And can you confirm that some of the words from the report are familiar to you? You used such words and, therefore, are familiar with them. So can you confirm that it is an UNCIVPOL memo?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Now you're speaking about the letter here dated the 13th to commissioner CIVPOL Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, both letters are dated the 13th of July. I would like to say this for the sake of the transcript and for your sake, I'm now referring to the letter you can see in my binder, and the number is 2D 000118. So it's a letter sent by Mr. Sorensen, and it is entitled "The Investigation into the Killing of Lieutenant Aguilar, the Mostar Spanish Battalion." Is that the document that you're actually looking at the moment?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, it is ma'am. And reading it over, there's nothing specific that triggers my memory in the wording here about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: A minute ago, you yourself said that you remembered that it was necessary to speak to the head of the HVO police, the chief of the HVO police, Mr. Filipovic, and the chief of the BH police, Mr. Maslesa. You were to talk to them about results of the investigations; is that correct? Do you remember it was necessary to have these conversations with them?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No. What I was reading here was that Mr. Sorensen, in his letter, said that it was part of the agreement stated that: "On completion of the investigation by both sides, Mr. Leo Bang Sorensen should consult with the chief of the HVO police, Mr. Filipovic, and chief of police BiH, Mr. Maslesa, on results of this inquiry." I'm just reading this from -- from the letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And my question is: Do you know that this is what had been agreed? Do you remember Mr. Sorensen telling you, in the course of the investigation, that this is the agreement that had been reached? It's precisely stated here. According to the agreement, at the end of the investigation, Mr. Sorensen should meet both of them. Do you remember such an agreement?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I -- I don't personally remember the agreement, and I'm sorry, my memory fails me about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember the last paragraph in the letter? It says: "UNCIVPOL is not in a position to fulfil this commitment because the CIVPOL investigation team has been transferred out of Mostar." Do you remember that happening on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No. And I -- when I first glanced at this and you had mentioned it, I agreed that it would be difficult not being allowed access into -- into East Mostar to meet with Chief Maslesa on the results. But I'm sorry, again, I do not remember it, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Once more, I would like to ask you to have a look at something. I'm not talking about the possibilities facing Mr. Sorensen. I just want to demonstrate that, on the basis of this report, we can see that on the 13th, when you drafted that report, the investigation quite obviously hasn't been concluded because Mr. Sorensen, on the very same day wrote, a letter in which he said that it wasn't possible for him to fulfil part of had his commitment, with regard to the investigation, because he did not meet both sides, "and I did not hear the results of the investigation." Sir, these two documents contradict each other, or what you can remember is in contradiction with this document, because you said that the report you typed out was a follow-up report. But this demonstrates that your investigation wasn't concluded on that date because in the last sentence it states that he wasn't in a position to carry out this obligation, that the UNCIVPOL was not in a position to fulfil its commitment because the investigation team had been transferred out of Mostar. I'm asking you whether you're aware of the fact that this team was moved out of Mostar, because it's quite obvious that this is a document that I have not seen. I'm asking you about what happened in the field. Was the UNCIVPOL investigation team moved out of Mostar, as is stated here?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I'll have to agree with you, ma'am, that, from what it does say there, that it would appear that there was going to be further investigation, but the last I remember of it was that previous one. But I do have to agree with you that, yeah, if he wasn't able to do that, that maybe somewhere down the line maybe they would continue to do more.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Given that you stated that this report was a final one, I put these questions to you. And, finally, with regard to this subject, have a look at the following document P 02723. It's the third there the bottom in my binder.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That was 2 Delta 0017, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: P 0 -- in my binder, P 02723. It's on the screen, but I hope you'll be able to find it in my binder. It's the third from the bottom, at the back.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I -- I believe I have it, ma'am. P 03027.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It's the third from the top.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, in my binder, it's the third from the top, 2723, 2723. P 02723. Have you found it now?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, I have, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court whether you are familiar with this kind of report? Have you already come across such reports? Did you come across such reports during your mission in Mostar? I'm just asking you about the form and about the first page. It's obvious that it's a report from the military police of UNPROFOR. It's about a serious military incident. I'm asking you a question about the form. I would like to know whether you had any contact with such reports from the UNPROFOR military police?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: It -- it is different from the form that we used in CIVPOL. I was involved, though, in the investigating -- the investigation of a shooting of a Spanish soldier that we determined was a suicide, and also military police investigators were involved. And I may have seen this same type of form in that investigation, but I cannot say for sure because it was so long ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. What confuses me somewhat - and I want to point this out for the sake of the Court. This is an exhibit or something that has been shown in this court already - but what confuses me is that, on the first page, we wouldn't really be able to see the date of this report. The report is also concerned with the death of Mr. Aguilar, but we can't see the date. Sir, could you find item 9 in the report which will help us determine the date concerned. Have a look at item 9. It's on the last page of the report. Let's see what the date is first of all, and then we'll deal with the contents. When you have found item 9, under A, on the last page, it says that this incident was investigated, and then there are some abbreviations that concern ranks and names. It says before their repatriation, before they returned. That was on the 29th of July, 1993. It says non-professional translators spent five weeks translating documents and statements in SpaBat. For the sake of the transcript, I'm putting this question to you: Although we don't have the date on the first page, it's quite obvious that this report must have been drafted after the 29th of July, 1993. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, ma'am. Item 9 in -- that I'm looking at here appears to be in Serbo-Croatian, and I don't -- I don't know what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You also have the English version. If not, then that's a serious mistake. I will provide you with that version, but you should have been provided with the English version in my binder at the outset.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Would it still be under P 02723?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes. That's the same number, and I suggest to you that it's item 9 on the last page of the report. In the English version, page 9 is not that legible; but if you have a look at the last page of the report, then it's the first, second, third, fourth, fifth sixth, seventh eighth paragraph from below or perhaps in the middle of the page itself. It's on the very last page of the document. It's actually on the screen. Have you got it now?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I think so, but I can't see which one is 9. There's some -- oh, I think I have it, yes. Where the one that says: "It must be stressed that, although there is a reason to believe that Lieutenant Aguilar was killed by a person from the HVO position, there is no direct physical or technical evidence available to confirm the suspicion." That is the one you're referring to, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, you're rushing somewhat. Have a look at 9(a). It's in the middle of the page, 9(a). We'll get to that conclusion too. First of all, I want to determine the date of the document. It's very important because it's not at the beginning of the document. Under (a), it says that this incident was "investigated by," and there are some abbreviations. It says it was investigated before the repatriation on the 29th of July, 1993. Non-professional translators took five weeks to translate statements and documents in SpaBat. So that's what I was referring to. Would you agree with me, if that's what it states in this report, then this very same report must have been drafted after the 26th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: It would appear so if that... [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So, sir, this report was drafted, or rather, the UNPROFOR military police drafted it -- let's say it was a day later on the 30th, but it was drafted 15 -- or rather, 17 days after the report that you said you had drafted and that you said was a final report. Let's have a look at what the conclusion of this report is. We had a look at what is stated under (a). Let's have a look what is stated under (b): "It wasn't possible to visit the scene of the shooting because of the fierce combat activity, and as a result no technical or relevant physical evidence could be collected."

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, I see where it says that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And under (c), it states the following: "It must be stressed that, although there is reason to believe that Lieutenant Aguilar was killed by a person from an HVO position, there is no direct physical or technical evidence available to confirm this suspicion." Item 10 states the following, and it's signed by the gentleman who drafted the report. It states: "Sir, this concludes my report. Should, however, any further information come to light, it will be the subject of an additional report." Sir, this report is one that perhaps you didn't see or hadn't seen before, but it does show that the UNPROFOR military police came to the conclusion -- or rather, concluded the investigation and stated that they could not find direct physical or technical evidence demonstrating that Lieutenant Aguilar was killed from an HVO position. Isn't that what is, in fact, stated in the report?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, it is, ma'am, and I would like to apologise. When I said that the final report was a final report that I remember having anything to do with, these other ones I had never seen. So -- and it's obvious that they were after the final that -- that I had something to do with.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And, finally, sir, one more question: After that final report of yours, dated the 13th of July -- or perhaps after this report from the end of July and the beginning of August, did you see anything or find anything out about this incident, apart from what is stated in this report? Did you have any information? Did you gain any information about this incident after, let's say, the 30th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I don't remember anything. As I say, the last thing I remember is the report that I had something to do with. And the rest of these things I have never seen before and I don't recall them, and I had no knowledge of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes that subject matter. Now I have another three questions about three subject matters. In your report of the 25th of August - we don't have to have a look at it, you can listen to me. It will be quicker - I'm referring to the report of the 25th of August, 1993. It concerns the entry of the convoy into Eastern Mostar. It's a very detailed report of over 10 pages. You and Mr. Sorensen signed it. I don't want to go into all the details of the report. But as far as you can remember, when you read this report, you can draw the conclusion that during those dramatic days, in Mostar, you had certain problems with UN civil mission and with their representatives. And there's detailed information about this in the report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct. There certainly were some conflict there between Mr. Sorensen and Mr. Benabou, and that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So that everything that is stated in the report demonstrates this, and this is the information you personally had. You were there during those days, so that's information that you personally had.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now could you have a look at document in the Prosecution binder, P 05861. P 05861, a document in the Prosecution's binder. This is your report on the incident. I've selected this one as an example. Have a look at form 3. That would be the third page of the report. At the top, it should say "Form 3." This is number 1. Tell me when you've found form 3. These are reports of your own, so I'm sure you're quite familiar with them?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Could you just give me a number again. I don't have a P 0 number, just a number. It was 58 --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: 5861. Let me see whether it's been correctly recorded in the transcript. You can then have a look at the transcript. It's in the Prosecution's binder. P 0 --

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I believe I have --

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I believe I have the report you're referring to. It's dated the 13th of October, a report that I wrote; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Correct. The 13th. The 13th of October. Have a look at it now. Have a look at Form 3. It's the third page in your report as far as I can see. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, I have, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, in the first paragraph, which I won't read out - I don't have the time - you can see that these individuals didn't want to reveal their identity, the individuals who gave these statements; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And it shows that the BH authorities, the civilian or military police, were aware of the identity of those individuals because they revealed their identity to them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I believe that the BiH police would know it, but they were concerned that reports in the United Nations going through what they considered their enemy territory might fall into the hands of the HVO and be used against them. So I think that was the reason why they didn't want to give their names in this report. I -- and I can't say for sure that the BiH did have them, but I feel they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, in your report, you state the following, and you signed the report, you say that: "If peace is ever established," I'm reading through the first paragraph, it says, "they hope," and you have the BH authorities in mind, "that they will conclude the investigation and file complaints against those who are responsible." You said: "They had the full names and addresses of the prosecutors." It seems that the BH authorities had the names of those who provided you with these statements. That's what this document shows. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, I don't see where you're reading that. And I remember at one time saying that the -- in my statement that I gave to the UN investigator when he came to Canada was that I thought that the BiH should have the names, but I don't have definite knowledge that they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, I wanted to be brief, but the first paragraph, Form 3, says: "Action taken: As already noted, this is an intelligence report alone. CIVPOL cannot take any action with regard to these crimes." Can you see that first sentence?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: In English in my report, and what I've written says: "Action taken: As noted before, this is an intelligence report only, and there is no action that CIVPOL is able to take regarding these crimes. The BiH have a file containing hundreds of similar war crimes. They are unable to take any police action concerning these crimes as present because they took place on the HVO controlled area and were committed by their enemy. "If peace is ever restored, they hope to complete their investigations and lay charges against those responsible." That's what the BiH hoped to do, and not just referring to the people I interviewed in this particular case, but that they had hundreds of complaints.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And then we have this sentence that follows. What do you go on to state? I'm having a look at the English version. It's identical. What is the following sentence? Please, tell us. Do read out your own report: "They have the full names." Isn't that what it says?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: "They have the full names and the addresses of the complainants. The four people CIVPOL were able to interview would only agree to give statements to the United Nations CIVPOL officers on the condition that they didn't have to give their names. They were -- they say they fear retaliation by the HVO, if they were ever to find out that they have made reports." And I believe that to be true.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
