utterances.text: Sir, sir, that's fine. That's fine. I didn't say anything to the contrary. All I wanted to say is that at the time that you gathered these statements, at the time you obtained statements from all the complainants as you call them, the BH side had their addresses and they were conducting investigations into war crimes at the time. But they said they couldn't conclude the investigation at that time because of the ongoing war. They said it would be continued at a subsequent date. So all I'm saying is that the BH authorities were aware of these individuals and probably had all the information that you had. Isn't that correct? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I believe that they would have had more information than I actually had.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, here you say in the first paragraph, you say that Forbes and Riggs spoke with these people alone and translation was provided by somebody from the B and H police. Is that what it says here? You did not use your own interpreter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, it was -- I used an interpreter from the East Mostar named Dragi [phoen]. And I'm sorry, after all these years, I cannot remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, excuse me. My time is taking. It says here that an interpreter from the BiH police was used for translation. So not a translation was used from your own mission, but a translator from the B and H police was used; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes. No, we couldn't bring in a translator. It was too dangerous for us to bring in the young lady who was our interpreter, so I used the one that was available in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And my final question: Sir, in your report - you don't have to look for it, just listen to me please. We will go faster - of the 13th [as interpreted] of September - and for the transcript, I would like to say that it's a report, P 00009 - you say, on the third page in English and the fifth page in Croatian, under the date of the 16th of September, you say that: "On this day, Observer Forbes returned with the convoy of the Spanish Battalion to East Mostar, to continue the job started during his previous visit." In the second paragraph, you say that: "The B and H police will place at their disposal an office in their building and Observer Forbes can use it as his own office." Mr. Forbes, can you please tell me, was this something that was allowed under the regulations or how can we say it? Did that made it possible to be objective if such a mission was located in the building of the civilian police on one side? Because I know where you were supposed to maintain your objectivity. And this position, was this something that was permissible? It's a little bit strange for me that you would be located in the building of the civilian police in Eastern Mostar.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: It never came to pass that I actually did get an office or ever did sleep there, but there was no rule prohibiting that, that I know of. And in most -- under the terms of CIVPOL, most of the other places, where the war situation wasn't so bad, we had monitors travelling with the police on all sides. And by being with the police, they were able to it observe what they were doing and to be able to -- to monitor their actions, to make sure that they were treating the minority fairly. If there had been any Croatian people or Serbian people in there, my myself, having contact with the police, I would have been able to watch and see and help to protect their rights. And this was one of the reasons why, in all of the different sectors and all of the different stations, this is the way that it was to be run, where you would actually be assigned with the police of that particular area. In this case, I'll have to admit that mention were a bit different because of the war situation, and there wasn't really any minority population there to protect, except for some prisoner of war. And I was allowed at one time to go, and I did inspect where they were being held and talk to those prisoners, as best I could, and saw the conditions they lived in.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I would just like to ask you -- I will be warned because I'm outside of my time that has been allocated to me. So at the end I would like to ask you -- I asked you something that is very, very simple. You said you were not in the best of relations with members of the HVO. Do you believe now from this distance that precisely that closeness that you are describing with the civilian police in Eastern Mostar could have been the reason -- could have been the reason, in fact, for that kind of intolerance shown to you by the HVO? Can you please tell me? Yes, yes. I did have the intention of asking you that question. You just said you visited several Croats that were in prison. Did you see citizens of eastern Mostar? Did you look for them? If you were supposed to protect the minorities there, didn't you have any information that there were some Croats living on the eastern side? Or perhaps there weren't any there. Didn't anyone give you any information? I see that you have a lot of information about what happened to Muslims or Bosniaks. Did anybody give you information that there were any Croats there, or did you get information that there weren't none there?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I didn't have any information. I couldn't locate any Croatian people there. The HVO never ever came to us and said, "We have people on that side. Can you check on them and look for them for us?" They never ever come forward to do that, and I didn't -- I never ran across any or saw any.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, did you receive information about possible Croats on the east side from police on the east side police that belonged to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, I didn't receive any information about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to continue on this topic. Unfortunately, I have used up my time, and I cannot continue. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And you used up all the time given to Mr. Pusic because you used nearly an hour. Next counsel, please. Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to clarify that I gave 15 minutes to Mr. Stojic's Defence, so maybe there has been some confusion about the calculation of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move on to Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. If I may just have the lectern, that would help me because I have some papers. Cross-examination by the Accused Praljak:

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Witness. Good day, Mr. Forbes.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm going to put some very technical matters to you, so I would like to have some brief answers. I'm going to ask you exclusively things that you do know. Not information from -- not second-hand or third-hand information, but only about things that you personally saw and know, and you can give your answers accordingly. We are going to go in order. At one point, you said that you saw, in Medjugorje, soldiers of the Croatian army from the 4th Corps. Can you please tell me, can you recall the date when this was, how many soldiers you saw?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I can't recall the -- I cannot recall the dates, sir, and I can't tell you the exact number, too. I remember a couple of trucks with tarps on them, and I could see that there were soldiers in the back; but how many, I don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You then said -- all right. You cannot tell how many soldiers there were. You said that they bore insignia of the 4th Corps. Do you know that there was never any 4th Corps that existed in Croatia? There was no 4th Corps in Croatia. What precisely did you see? Did you see HV insignia, or did you just see some coat of arms that you don't know anything about, but that seemed to resemble some sort of motorised formation?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: The -- the insignia that I saw, and those were the soldiers that were in the cab, was just the Croatian flag -- shoulder flash without the HV or HVO on it, and what -- the 4th Corps, what I remember was the crest on the side of the truck, saying "4th Corps." My memory's quite vague on it. It's been so long ago, but what I remember is it looked like a motorcycle gang crest than the type of military crest that I would be familiar with in Canada, with coats of arms and whatnot, and also from information that I received from people who had told me that they were 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to ask you -- there is no 4th Corps. Again, please, do not give me information that you got from others. Can you please only specifically answer about what you saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you should not discuss with the witness. If the witness says he's seen it, that's it. The rest you are doing is you are giving testimony on what the army was, and that's not your task. You have to ask questions, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Please do not discuss, but exercise cross-examination properly. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I am doing that Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think there was a problem in translation. Mr. Praljak asked the witness to respond to what he saw himself and not about things that he heard, and it seems that there is some sort of a misconnection there because then you intervened, and Mr. Praljak, I think, quite properly responded to what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, according to the interpretation, Mr. Praljak was giving testimony on whether there was or not a 4th Corps in the Croatian army, and that's giving information. That's not asking a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated] THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I'm asking if the gentleman knows the fact that if there is a 4th Corps in the Croatian army or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not personally know the make-up of the Croatian army, at that time, either in 1993. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please, sir, the question is very simple. And if you help me, we will proceed very simply without a lot of explanations. It's a simple question: Do you know if there were corps in the Croatian army, and among them the 4th Corps, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I would have to say no.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Then say "no," if you have to say that. I'm asking you the next question. On the 28th of June, you came to Medjugorje in 1993. Do you know that on the 30th of June, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the area of the northern Logor and the northern part of Mostar, Crveno Polje, carried out an attack and captured those areas towards the north, linked up with the forces from Jablanica and captured Rastani? Does this mean anything to you? Do you know this or not?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Are you aware that, on the 13th of August, it began a large attack from Blagaj towards the south, towards Buna; that Brdo Kicini [phoen] was captured; and that the HVO, after a few days of fighting, managed to take back those positions? Are you aware of this or not?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I do remember something about that, yes, but my memory on it is very vague. But I do remember that the BiH had -- went on the offensive. They captured some land. But not having any heavy weapons or anything, they weren't able to hold it and the situation was basically the same as it was before in the end, is the way I understood it, but I could be wrong, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Forbes, please. I am asking a precise question, so just please answer what I'm asking you. Here is the next question: You're claiming that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had no heavy weapons. You said that several times. Please, tell me. Where do you have the information that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the 4th Corps, did not have heavy weapons? Did you directly have insight into those facts or is this information coming from third- or fourth-hand?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No. What I meant, and I think what I did say, was I never saw any heavy weapons on the BiH side in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we believe that, based on the fact that you didn't see these weapons, this weaponry does not exist? Is that what you're saying? If I didn't see the weapons, they don't exist? Is that what your case is, or are you just saying, "I did not see any heavy weaponry?"

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I object to the question. It's not a fair question, Your Honours. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Okay. Did you see the weapons? No, you didn't. Did you know if the heavy weaponry existed or not?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I did not see any heavy weapons on their side. I did not observe any heavy weapons being fired from their side, and that's all I can say on the matter, sir. I don't know. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me if you know how many soldiers were there in the 4th Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina that was stationed in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know how many civilian police officers of the army in Bosnia and Herzegovina there were in Mostar, in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, sir. I don't have that number.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: According to your testimony, is it correct that civilian policemen in Eastern Mostar wore camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct. They had asked if I could help get them blue serge material and light blue material for shirts, but they --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness - he's asked a specific question - that he be permitted to finish his answer. I mean, he was giving a relevant answer, and I don't think it's fair to cut him off halfway through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Forbes, if you have not completed answering, please continue it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have completed it, Your Honour. They asked for blue material to make uniforms, but they weren't able to get any. And the police I saw were wearing more of a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Forbes, I'm somewhat amazed because Mr. Praljak had put a question to you as to the number of civilian police members, and your answered you didn't know. Looking at the documents produced by the Prosecutor this morning, we can see that you had very close links with the two people who were in charge of the police. You even said in one document that one had asked you if his wife could go to Denmark. So upon reading all this, I thought that you must have been speaking for hours with the heads of the police, and I can understand this all the better since you yourself had been a policeman in your country. But during these conversations you had with them, did those men not tell it you how many there were police officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The number of police officers in their force never did come up. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like you, once again, just to understand that this kind of cross-examination that is a little bit perhaps causing some kind of disturbance is just a question of time available.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that on the 20th of September, 1993 - and in your testimony, you mentioned that as a date when there was a major bombing on Mostar - that on that day, as part of the offensive Neretva 93 -- first of all, did you ever hear of an offensive of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina by the name of Neretva 93?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I don't recall that name, sir. You were asking about how I'd heard about the offensive that was going on in that period of the 20th through until the 28th, when I finally got in there. It was information that was coming from the United Nations UNMO people about heavy fighting, and my commander, station commander, wouldn't allow me to go in because of that fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know that, on the 20th of September, 1993, a major attack began by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina on western Mostar, on Hum Hill, except for its northern part. Do you know -- do you personally know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. I knew there was heavy fighting going on. But as far as tactics and who was attacking who, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know that the commander of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it's southern sector, Satovic [phoen], writes in his book that on that day they had excellent support from the artillery of the army of Republika Srpska. Thus, on that day, the army of Republika Srpska fired from its artillery at the town of Mostar, western Mostar. They talk about quite substantial support. Do you know anything about that or not?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. I didn't read that book. I missed that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, my question had to do with whether you yourself had seen anything of that when you were out in the field in Medjugorje. I wasn't specifically asking you whether you knew about this from this particular book. The book is not so relevant, but did you yourself know anything about this, yes or no? No?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, sir. I never witnessed any incoming heavy fire from the BiH side at any time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please reconstruct the following things: According to what I read in documents from the Prosecution - and I cannot point out to you all of them - you were in Mostar for the first time for one day, on the 28th of August; and then on the 25th of August, you came with a convoy until the 29th; and then you were there on the 13th of September for one day; the 14th -- the 16th of September, 1993; the 4th and the 5th, on the morning, you came back; and then on the 8th and the 11th of October, you were in Mostar on two occasions. Other than the dates I specifically mentioned, were you in Eastern Mostar at any other time; if yes, can you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: In that time period that you were just referring to there, sir, I did go in on the 4th, and I was in -- overnight on the 4th and the 5th, and, of course, as you've mentioned the 8th and the 11th. And from that period that you mentioned till then, those were the only times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I was in later if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may draw your attention to line 16, Mr. Praljak. You say on the 28th of August and then on the 25th. Probably you wanted to name a different date the first time, the 21st; is that correct? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. The 21st of August, because of the hospital; the 25th of August, four days; the 13th of September; the 14th of September; the 4th; and then on the 5th in the morning, you returned; and then on the 8th and the 11th of October. That is what you mentioned. I'm not going to go into that any more. So these are the periods --

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I was there for the 7th and the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. This is in 1993, October. The 7th and the 11th of October, 1993. Now I would like to ask you this, while we are waiting for the map to be shown, 3D 01064, 3D 01064. While we're waiting for that map to appear on the monitor, you have that in the binder, but it will be good in colour on the screen, sir. Until we're waiting for that, can you please look at the map to the right of you, behind you, the big map where we see the town of Mostar. The gentleman from our team here will give you marker and you can mark on this map the Hum hill, and can you try to mark where the positions of the army and Bosnia and Herzegovina were in Mostar and where the positions of the Croatian Defence Council were.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I will try my best. I'm sorry, sir. I can't pick out specifics on this map. I have to apologies for my eyesight not being as good as it used to be, but it's very confusing to me just looking at that. And I couldn't, in all fairness, actually point out the different positions from 14 years ago, because --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: -- My memory --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: -- Mr. Forbes. I quite understand. Can you look at this map here now. Based on what you know - and you talked about some military matters quite a lot - can you approximately indicate the positions of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Mostar from the south to the north, where the positions of the Croatian Defence Council were, and where the positions the army of Republika Srpska were? You've said a lot about how there was firing, what was firing, at whom there was firing. So let us see how much you actually know about the military situation at the time you were there. If you don't know, you will just tell us that you are unable to make these markings. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] It would be better if we could perhaps zoom in more on the map, and if we can focus on Mostar itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Looking at the map, I can -- I can make it out a little bit better, now that this is bigger.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can -- from looking at this map here, and -- can you just make it a little teeny bit bigger. From where I was, and in Medjugorje and whenever I patrolled the areas that I patrolled, it was always in HVO-controlled territory, other than when I was on the east side of Neretva in East Mostar, which was BiH at that time. I had never been anywhere in this area where the Serbs were stationed, and I have no personal knowledge of what their locations were. I don't know where all of the HVO military positions were. The UNMOs and ourselves used to be turned back when we got close to any -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Forbes, I am sorry, but we're going back to the military observers again. They have been here and they have testified. So please can we draw the following conclusion, it's quite simple: You, from your position, as a civilian policeman, were not aware of where the Republika Srpska had its positions. You didn't know where the BH army had its positions toward the north and south of Mostar, and you don't know exactly where the HVO positions were; is that correct? These were things that you were not aware of.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Only my personal -- the only personal knowledge I have are the ones that I saw, and, no, I would not know where all of the HVO positions were or where all of the BiH positions were because, you know, I was only confined to a certain area. I had to -- once we got in the APC, I basically had to go on foot. So the area that I could cover and actually have a view of was quite limited.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, sir. I don't doubt that, but what I want to know is with regard to the north of Mostar, since you say yourself that Mostar was encircled. Well, can you tell me, to the north of Mostar, in Bijelo Polje, across the Bijelo bridge, Vrapcici, et cetera, well, was the route free towards Jablanica and Konjic there? Did you ever pass through that way? Did you ever go to the north of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, sir, I never drove to the north. We were always stopped by the HVO roadblocks and not permitted to go up that way. The only time I was basically north of Mostar, when I was in Bosnia, was when I would fly from Split into Sarajevo by air.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir. Sir, on the 30th of June - and the Judges know this - the BH army took northern Mostar. Can you tell me the date when you tried to move from the north of Mostar and were stopped by an HVO patrol? We have to be quite precise. We're before a tribunal here, and very precise matters are being decided on here. When you went to the north, you say you were stopped by an HVO patrol. When?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact date, sir, as I don't have a note on it, and it was 14 years ago. But I distinctly remember in July of that year, before I was actually able to get into Mostar, attempting on several occasions to get north, and I remember on one occasion driving north. We were allowed partway into -- we were allowed to -- the overlook would be on the north part of Mostar, and there was a high ground there and a good view down into the city, and that was the farthest I ever got or were allowed to go bill the HVO. And that would have been in July of that year, sir, but the exact date. I'm sorry, I can't remember after these years.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. As to whether it was in July, well, the Judges will compare this with other testimony and the situation in Mostar in July 1993. My following question, sir, is follows: Have a look at the following document. I'll ask you about the house of the military observer, the house hat you slept in. The document concerned is P 09303 [as interpreted]. P 09303. Mr. Forbes, do you remember that the house was in Eastern Mostar, and it was quite high up on a hill below the main road from Sarajevo to Metkovic?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes. I remember this house. This was the UNMOs' house. Their call-sign was Mike 5, as I recall. This is not where we lived. We lived in a pension in Medjugorje that belonged to an HVO soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Forbes. Mr. Forbes, unfortunately, since time is short, we can't go into all of this. My question is quite simple: What we can see before us, well, was it part of the house facing north? I want to determine certain logical and mathematical facts. My question is as follows: Is this part of the house facing north?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I believe it is, yes. It's kind of dark and a little hard to make out, but I believe that, yes, that would be on the north side.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That's better now.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, that's a better picture. It is a little more restricted, but it does appear that it's the north side.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, listen to this simple question: We can see that it's been hit by bullets, and is this part of the house facing north? You are a professional policeman. You were involved in investigations. So could this house be hit from any of the HVO positions, according to the information you have?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: This is -- I believe this is the north-facing wall. Again, I'm not just exact on how the house was situated, but I remember more to the west wall. And I remember sleeping in the upper floor, and there was sandbags on the west wall.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'll show you some other photographs of the northern part. Let's have a look at P 1000 [as interpreted], P 1000. This is a photograph that another, a different witness showed us. It's a photograph of the same house, but it represents the part of the house facing west. So it would have been possible for the HVO to fire on this part of the house. Do you know what the distance was between that house and the first HVO lines, well, let's say at the Bulevar? Do you know what the distance was between the house and the first HVO lines that the HVO had at the Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's -- that is the west wall I recognise, or what I assume to be the west wall. And the exact distance to the HVO lines from there, I don't know what they are. I was never able to take any kind of measurement or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I understand that you didn't have the possibility of taking measurements, but you're drawing a conclusion, and I ask you how. Can you show us on this house where we can see the sandbags that were hit? And given the distance and kinetic force, et cetera, can you show us where the wall or the ceiling were penetrated, and where some kind of a picture was hit? So where did the bullet come through? Where can you see significant damage to the sandbags, to the sand coming out? So show me, after this intense shooting, how many bullets hit the facade of the house; and show me where the bullets, which bullets actually penetrated the wall; and show me which sandbags were ripped apart as a result of the shooting?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Do you know when this picture was taken, sir? Was this taken in late November or when was it taken? It may have been taken long before I was ever there and long before this incident that I described ever happened. So I can't -- I can't comment on that at all, because I don't know when it was taken, you know. That picture might have been taken shortly the day that those sandbags were put up there before anything had happened there. So, I'm sorry, I can't help you on that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Forbes, well, the logics is quite correct. And if we followed such logics, I would be very happy. But this demonstrates, this proves that -- or rather, it's an exhibit tendered by the Prosecution in order to demonstrate what was going on there. My questions are simple. I only had two questions. Where was the damage do the house? Where did the bullet penetrate the western side? What was the distance to the front line and to the north? Since you were there and you're a professional policeman, you could answer such questions before doing anything else. Could the bullets to the north -- northern side have come from any HVO positions? Well, these are my questions. Try and answer them if you can.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I'll do my very best, sir. As far as the damage to the outside, I can't comment on that at all because I don't know when this picture was taken. All I can tell you is, from my personal knowledge, I was sleeping inside the house. I heard the bullets hitting the sandbagged area outside of the house. I remember, when I woke up in the morning, that there were four bullets that had come through into the house that hadn't been there the night before when I went to sleep, and that one of these bullets had hit a picture of a deer. I recall this -- the painting. There was a scene of three what appeared to be me white-tailed deer in it, and it caught my attention because I am a hunter back in Canada. And it reminded me of a scene in Canada, and one of these deer was hit above in the painting where this Egyptian UNMO had been sleeping. But on the outside, I never did go around and inspect what kind of damage there was on the outside. And, as I said, without being able to know when this picture was being taken, I feel I'm not able to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may just one question. Can you on this picture indicate behind which opening you were sleeping.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Like I say, I was on the inside sir, and I think it's probably in the area of where these first sandbags were. But in my memory, I believe there were more sandbags. At that time, they had added more sandbags to it and more of an area was covered by sandbags. But I would, again, without being able to see the inside of the house, it's really very difficult for me to say, with any accuracy, where exactly I was on the inside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. It's going to be time for the break and, in fact, you've used up quite a lot of time. Do you have more questions? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we agreed that I would have 15 minutes from Mr. Pusic's Defence. Ms. Senka -- well, I don't know about that. But I have a few more technical questions, if I may put them to the witness. I don't know how to deal with such matters. You hear a lot of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise. I wouldn't want to prejudice Mr. Praljak's Defence. I got a bit carried away. I wasn't pay attention. So perhaps he could be given 15 minutes that I used up, and perhaps you could subsequently take away those 15 minutes from my further cross-examination. It's my mistake. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's now 4.00. We're going to have a 20-minute break, and then Mr. Praljak will have another 15 minutes and that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you have 15 minutes. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Forbes -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Could we go into private session, please, because there are some documents I would like to tender.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption. Your Honours, we're back in open session. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: According to your information, can you tell us, where the 4th Corps of the ABiH command was, where the command of the 1st Mostar Brigade was, where the command of the military police was, where the command of the civilian police was, the civilian police in camouflage uniforms, the logistics base of the ABiH? Do you know where they were located in the eastern part of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: The -- I was told, at one time, this one big stone building had been their headquarters of the 4th corps, and it was on one of my subsequent visits in there. The first time I was in there, on the 21st and the second time between the 25th and the 28th of August, it was still in good condition. But the next time I came in, it was all blown to pieces and that was object Tita Malesa Street. Am I saying at that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, please. Marsal Tito, yes. Sir, please answer my question precisely, without providing any additional explanations as to how things were damaged. My question is as follows: Do you know that when crossing the Marsal Tito bridge or the Old Bridge, well, there were ABiH soldiers who crossed over the bridge and they were carrying arms and had ammunition. Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I have no personal knowledge of that, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that, when crossing the Marsal Tito bridge, they often used the protection of certain international organisations, vehicles, et cetera, and they crossed the bridge by walking behind a vehicle that belonged to some international organisation? I'm referring to the ABiH. Are you familiar with this fact?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge of that, and I've never seen anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In one of your reports, it says we -- or rather, it says that the SpaBat would park its armoured vehicle in the vicinity of a very high building in order to reduce the possibility of being hit by artillery shells. Are you familiar with the trajectory of a mortar shell if it's fired from a distance of three or four kilometres? Did you ever analyse the trajectory of a mortar shell, where it came from, from the HVO position or from Republika Srpska position? Did you ever carry out an analysis of such a kind?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I have a limited knowledge of the trajectory. And as a bomb technician in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, I have been on courses on post-blast investigations. And I would note from the seat of the explosions of some of the mortars, that would hit in the street, I could tell they came from the west due to the fragmentation pattern around the -- the crater at the seat of the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But let's say, if the vehicle was parked by a house and the parabolic trajectory from the HVO side, well, did you ever tried to calculate whether the trajectory was such? You say that two mortars, for example, on both sides of the vehicle exploded; and after such an event, did you go to see, to determine whether such a trajectory was possible, whether it was possible for a shell to fall on both sides of the vehicle in a narrow street, for example, and if the vehicle is next to a building?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: When I was pulled in to the APC, by the others that were in there, just as the second mortar hit, my memory of it is like being in the middle of the fireball and I had been hit in the flak jacket with pieces of shrapnel; and after that, checking that my pants weren't full, I didn't go anywhere looking for the trajectory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have a comment. In answering a question, you've said something very important here that no other witness, thus far, has said, which is that you are a bomb technician and a technician with knowledge of explosives. And you've just said that, when you examined the impact of this mortar and examined the pieces of shrapnel, you were able to determine where the mortar had come from. And you said that it came from the west, in your opinion. Is that what you have just said? Did I understand correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You misunderstood, Your Honour. Not that I was talking about those two particular mortars that came in and straddled the APC I was on. I was talking about in the parking position behind the buildings, the mortars that I had seen struck in the street, the craters that were located there, and I was able to examine them. And I also recall, on one occasion, a mortar hitting on the roof across the street above us. If it had have been 30 more feet, short it would have landed right in the middle of the street where all the people were gathered to get their water. But I think the -- misunderstanding was that I was speaking about those craters in the road, and not the ones when the APC that I was on was straddled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, but in the street, the craters in the street, on the basis of your technical analysis, you believe that the shots came from the west; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell me how you establish that it came from the west? You're talking about these two that I'm talking about. You didn't look at the trajectory, how it could have come there, what the distance was. I don't see those two shots that I am talking about. Did you correct them and came to the conclusion that they both fell from the side of the HVO and not from the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's -- that's a fair question. I didn't do an investigation and try and find out exactly where those two shells had come from that we're speaking of there now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the shell that hit the roof, when a shell hits a roof, can you please tell me when it strikes and all you can see after that are shards or fragments. Can you please tell me how you determine that it came from the west and not from the side of the Republika Srpska? Did you establish that it did come from the west, from the part of the HVO, or did you just establish that it came from the west?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: It came from the west. It whistled over the building and, it came down in an arc from the west and hit onto the roof.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. His Honour, Judge Antonetti, asked you when people were in line for water and they were running past and so on first. Can you please tell me where exactly was this in Eastern Mostar? What is that part called, the street? Where was this?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That would be on Marsal Tito Street. If you're familiar, sir, with the hospital and where it was located, the former library, as I understand, well, just a block down, there is a fairly wide intersection, and then there's a building where the -- they used to unload a lot of the flour and things like that. And we were just a little bit to the south of that, and that's where we were located, in those two big buildings that were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Please, when you were there and you turned towards the west, which HVO position and which building were you able to see optically as a place that that place could be hit? Which HVO building or Hum? How far are they and which one of them had the optical visibility? When you enter Mostar - and I was there for two years and after that came to visit my parents - what can he seen from that street towards the west in relation to any position of the HVO, and what would be the distance from there to there?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: From where we were on the APC there, you wouldn't be able to see any of the positions to the west; however, that particular mortar that came over, it came over. And I could see it coming over the building from the west and hitting at an angle from the west on top. And this being the street full of some women and children, all Muslim women and children, and the odd off-duty soldier who was there, too, I didn't think the HVO would be shooting in their own direction there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So what you are saying is that the soldiers were constantly mixed, intermingled with the civilian population on the eastern bank, that they were together with the civilians. They were sleeping there. You say you saw some 20 people. They went running past. Is that true or not that you were constantly seeing groups of soldiers walking around the streets of Eastern Mostar with weapons? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No. You would -- you would occasionally see one or two soldiers with weapons going. But when I'm saying that some people that would have on the brown camouflage uniforms, they apparently must have been off duty because they weren't carrying sidearms. But, occasionally, you would see a soldier or a group of soldiers going up the street to a different location, but it wasn't a common thing to see them mixing with the civilian population there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you have already used 45 minutes, and normally your time is up. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] My last question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My fellow Judge says, well, it is up. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] This is my final question, and, Your Honour, you took up two minutes. Last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: On the 25th of August, 1993, a convoy with humanitarian aid entered Mostar. Did you see me in that convoy sitting on the first APC from Citluk until the very first check-point on the approach to the city? Did you see me sitting there with that convoy, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing you, sir. No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please, the Judges saw your report and the reports of five other organisations here. Can you, as a representative or a public contact, how is it possible that five reports do not mention the commander waving his arms about and saying something there and sitting on the APC and waving it through, allowing it to pass through to Mostar? Is that some kind of failing, or was it something that was intentional? How was it possible that this was not mentioned in any report? Were you a good rapporteur then or not?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: You're -- you're talking about when the convoy was allowed to leave Citluk and start to proceed at Citluk? Is that where you're speaking of, sir?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Okay. I was on an APC further toward the back; and once it started moving, I believe I was sitting down inside the APC, and I didn't see exactly who was directing traffic or anything at that time. There had been some rocks being thrown by children and what on, so that's why I was sitting down inside the APC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Forbes, a follow-up question. Apparently, Mr. Praljak argues that if this convoy was able to proceed, it was thanks to him. Now, how is it possible that if he had a positive contribution, that the internationals present on the spot did not mention in a report, that it was due to his intervention as an HVO commander that the humanitarian convoy was able to proceed and meet its requirements?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I say, I was just a passenger going in with the Spanish. I had no involvement in the negotiations to get it released from Citluk, and I didn't -- I didn't see him. I don't -- I can't comment on what the others said or what they reported, but I didn't see it myself, sir, Your Honour. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Forbes. Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Next counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have two corrections for the transcript, and we can register that right away if I may be allowed. On page 130, 1-3-0, line 2, the exhibit number is P 0903. The correct number should be P 09303. Yes. And then on page 131, line 4, it says P 1000, and it should be four 0's because it's P 10000. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Forbes. You told us today, Mr. Forbes, if I understood you correctly, that from Muslim police and the population of Eastern Mostar, you found out that the HVO attacked the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that that is how the clashes between these two armies began. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, that's what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I conclude from that that you did not talk about the beginning of the conflict between the HVO and the ABiH with the Croatian police or the citizens of Western Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, ma'am. I don't recall having a conversation with anyone telling me from that -- from that side where or how it had started.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. In response to Mr. Flynn's question about the bad relationship of the HVO towards the UN agencies, you answered today how these UN agencies attempted to supply the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina with food and humanitarian aid; that the HVO, for that reason, considered that those agencies were aiding the enemy; and that this was more or less the reason of the attitude of the HVO towards the UN agency. This was recorded on page 36 of today's transcript. Am I correct in stating this, Mr. Forbes?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: If I said that about supplying the army of the BiH, then I misspoke because the UN agencies were trying to supply the civilian population of East Mostar and not the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm going to tell you exactly what you said. You mentioned neither the civilians nor the army; but you said on page 36, line 4, I will read did in English: "[In English] Because we were trying to take in supplies of food and humanitarian relief to the B and H."

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's correct that I said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So B and H, as a rule, you used when you refer to the army.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just used to refer to that as the Muslim side. I didn't realise that it was specifically referring to the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Forbes, can you please tell us, describing the task of the civilian police of the UN today, you said that its tasks were to oversee treatment of the local police towards the national minorities, and that is why I was asking was it the task of your institution, of your agency, in any way to assist the local population in supplying them with food and humanitarian relief in general?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That wouldn't be our primary mission. Our primary mission would be actually to monitor the police. However, we had to -- whenever the situation arose, we would natural tell the sister agencies. The ones that could help with the problem most, the information would be passed on to them, and that's why we would do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we agree - and I think that this is not in dispute - that other UN agencies were in charge of supplies and that you were a kind of support for the UNHCR and other similar agencies or institutions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I would say that's a correct statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Forbes, in reference to the shelling of Eastern Mostar, you told us quite a lot, and I am trying to summarise everything you said in three items; and then we will see if I understood you correctly. First, in the period that you were there, according to the reports which we saw today, the shelling of Eastern Mostar was frequently quite strong, savage, heavy; that there were periods when a thousand shells an hour rained over Eastern Mostar; and that there were periods when 20 projectiles and minute dropped on Eastern Mostar. Second, as for the targets, you said that most of the shelling was in the civilian sections, and that there were no military facilities and no military targets hit. And, third, that you did not see the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina opening heavy fire. Did I correctly summarise your statements referring to the shelling?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I would like to move into private session, because I would like to try to compare these witnesses' statements with some documents that are protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I think it is rather to put something in correct perspective. Ms. Alaburic has suggested that the witness had said that they were taking supplies to the BiH, but one has to read the whole sentence. The question was: Was there a bad relationship? And the answer was: "Yes, it was. I believe that they felt that because we were trying to take in supplies to the BiH we were assisting their enemy." So the witness has not asserted that they have done this, but he has said that they believe that we did it. So there is no contradiction on what he said on cross-examination to what he said earlier on page 36, lines 3, 4, and 5. I think that was a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that we clarified that the witness said the Muslim side, primarily civilians, and that there was a correction in the sense of army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But my modest knowledge of English says that his statement still should be interpreted differently, because he says... [No interpretation]... from which it arises that they were trying to bring in food and supply the population, and that he thinks that the HVO, because of that, let's say, had a relatively bad relationship or attitude towards the UN agencies. I think we clarified that, but thank you very much in any case. Your Honours, if we can move into private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of my contact would more be with the deputy chief, Mr. Salko Zuljevic rather than Mr. Ramo Maslesa. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What is important to me is just to tell me, when we're talking about the B and H police in this instance, we're talking about the civilian police, and when we're referring to these two gentlemen. This was in Eastern Mostar, and so it was your mandate mostly to be in contact with the civilian police. Am I right on that?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is a question already put to you by Mr. Praljak today, and you said that there was a problem with the uniforms because the civilian police in Eastern Mostar wore camouflage uniforms and did not have the classic blue uniforms that a regular civilian police force would need to have; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. They asked if I could help to get material so that they could make that type of uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, if you know, whether in general, in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in the area of Eastern Mostar, it was known that the provision of the army with uniforms was rather worse than better, and that there were situations also when people who did not belong to any unit actually wore uniforms, that it was some sort of trend? Are you aware of this occurrence?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes. There was a number of people who had army-type uniforms on but no insignia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that members of the military police of the HVO, regular members who actually belonged to the military police force, had to have insignia on their uniforms which stated "VP HVO," white cross belts, and badges? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I didn't know that that was a regulation, but it sounds quite reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I hope that I will not have to open up documents and, therefore, I will not have to move into closed session, because I notice you remember well the four incidents that you discussed previously with the Prosecutor. So all I will say for the transcript is these are document 505730 and document -- P 05730, and document 505800 [as interpreted]. These are those instances of expulsions from apartments. These were two cases. The transcript has it down wrongly; P, like Poland, 05800. These were two instances of expulsions from apartments. In both cases, they -- there were situations in which persons came introducing themselves as members of some unit, or not introducing themselves at all, wearing uniforms without insignia. Do you recall that this was like that in reference to these incidents?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that when a person appears at the door who does not introduce themselves and they're wearing a uniform without insignia, or it's a group of people wearing different uniforms and the persons are not known to the victims, that it is practically impossible to identify those people as members of a specific unit and to put a name -- first and last name to them? I said practically impossible and not practically possible. This is a correction of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes. If they didn't know the personally, it would be hard to identify them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You also responded to questions today of the first attorney who put questions to you, my learned friend, Ms. Nozica, that these persons in these four incidents did not want to give you their names because they did not wish to be identified by the HVO authorities; and from that I draw, the conclusion that they did not wish to report what happened to them to the HVO authorities but exclusively to the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Eastern Mostar and later to you, of course, without providing their names in order to protect themselves. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And this then means that the HVO authorities did not know about these four incidents at the time that you were drafting your report. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I don't believe they did, no. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: One of these incidents, and I will ask to move into private session because I will have to mention some details if this is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, I hope that on the occasion of your arrival in Eastern Mostar you acquainted yourself with the structure of the civilian police in Eastern Mostar. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I didn't know -- as I say, as I testified earlier, I didn't know exactly how many police officers they had. I knew who the chief was, who the deputy chief was, who the chief of detectives was, but I really didn't have a knowledge of their rank structure or how many people they had and if they had different specialised units and whatnot. I didn't know anything of those things.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know what the extent of the duties of the civilian police in Eastern Mostar was in wartime conditions?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: In wartime conditions, I realise it would be very, very hard to carry out proper investigations the way you would do in peacetime, but I would expect that they would be -- as a civilian police, that they would investigate crimes committed against the different people within their jurisdiction, try and solve these crimes, and bring the people involved to justice. And I know, I realise, too, that in that sort of a situation probably the courts were shut down, and there was a -- it would be quite difficult to do a lot of the things that would normally be done in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I agree with you. My next question is: When you talked as a professional policeman with officials of the civilian police in Eastern Mostar or police staff in Eastern Mostar, did they present to you the results of their work? For example, the number of criminal acts, protection of property, protection of persons, protections of goods, traffic control, and other general crimes. Were you able to oversee their results of work, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No. When we were able to talk, we would be -- we would be discussing cases that we had information on and were trying to find out about. And when we did have time to just spend some time talking as police officers, as policeman to policeman, it was Mr. Salko Zuljevic who -- I found his police stories very interesting, and it was obvious to me that he took great pride in being a good policeman and solving a difficult case.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you remember at least one of those serious cases that the deputy chief, Salko Zuljevic, solved at that time in Eastern Mostar?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I remember one case he was telling me about. It was a fraud investigation, and him and Mr. Sejic also worked on it. And the suspect had torn up some documents and flushed them down a septic tank, and they dug up that septic tank and got into it and recovered the documents. And I thought that was quite dedicated.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you ever ask Mr. Zuljevic - Zuljevic, since I know him personally so I do know what his name is - did you ever ask him about the process of Croats and Serbs leaving Eastern Mostar? Did you ever discuss that subject?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: The process of Croats and Muslims leaving Eastern Mostar? Oh, and Serbians leaving it? No. I don't recall a conversation about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. And you said that your task was to protect minorities in certain environments, so who did you protect then? Who was to be protected? That's what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: We would have protected anybody. If somebody had come to us with a complaint, if somebody from the HVO side, for example, who were concerned about relatives in East Mostar and felt they might have been in some sort of trouble, you know, we would have gladly gone and checked on them and made sure that they're being treated fairly. But I honestly can say I never actually met any Croatian or Serbian people in East Mostar when I was there, but we certainly would have if we had received a complaint from someone we would have went and see them, if we could find them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, with regard to Eastern Mostar, do you know how many Croats, Serbs and Muslims, lived there before the war, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you didn't know that. Did you at that time in Eastern Mostar only several dozen Croats lived in Eastern Mostar, and apparently you did not succeed in meeting a single one of them.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Sir, it just has jogged my memory. I do remember meeting one elderly Croatian woman. Would you like me to explain that?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I don't have the time. I have a few more questions for you. In the western part of Mostar, was there a UN Civilian Police station?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's where our station was located; not in the western part, no, in Medjugorje. We didn't have a UN Civilian Police station in Western Mostar. We weren't able to get in there. The guys that were working on that side, they weren't able to go into West Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you ever meet any officials from the civilian police from Western Mostar during that period of time and anywhere and at any time?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir. And in the period when I first arrived there through July, I met a number of HVO police and had had some dealings with them on a couple of investigations. One of them walls the suicide of a Spanish soldier. Another time, down in Capljina, I visited the police station down there to check on some -- two German nationals who had been arrested, and went down there to see if we could effect their release and they were released the next day, and they had not been mistreated or anything like that. There were other occasions, too, that I met with some policemen and --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And my last question. You did meet officials of the civilian police from Western Mostar, from Western Herzegovina. What was your impression of them? Were these people professionals when it came to carrying out their duties?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: In the case of the suicide of the Spanish soldier, I thought that they did a very good job. They were quite professional in that case. And on a one-to-one basis with the different policemen I met, I didn't really experience very much difficulty with them, and we were able to achieve what we were trying to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have any questions, Mr. Ibrisimovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. I do have some questions. I won't be long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, we speak the same language so we'll have to sort of have a pause, and I do tend to speak quickly and sort of fire away rapidly with the questions. So let's give the interpreters a break after this long day. First, let me introduce myself. My name is Michael Karnavas; with me is Suzana Tomanovic. We represent Dr. Jadranko Prlic. Now, you've indicated in -- you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: The statement in Canada that I gave to Investigator Cameron?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In that statement, you indicated that you did not have any personal dealings with any of the religious dealers in Medjugorje, nor with the HVO military leaders; you said that?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you say "HVO military leaders," is that in general or are you just specifically speaking about that particular location?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I didn't -- you know, I wasn't meeting with them or negotiating with them or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would it be also fair to say that you didn't meet with any HVO civilians?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Oh, I met a number of HVO civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Authorities? Yes. As I say, we dealt with them on those cases I just mentioned. Another case was one time I had my flak jacket stolen, and I went to the -- the police station in Citluk and that was the first time I realised there was actually a branch of the police that looked after tourist-type claims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you're talking about authorities, you're talking about police authorities?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Would it be fair to say this was your first venture outside of Canada on a mission like this?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you are a trained police officer, not a trained military person?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Is it also fair to say that your knowledge, albeit you did get one week of training, was rather limited on the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On the conflict that was -- that was ongoing at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, in fact, when you arrived you -- sorry. When you arrived, and that would have been in Mostar, it would have been sort of at the end of June 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I spent a month before that in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Different location?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Different situation?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Different players?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when you got there, on 28 June 1993, is it fair to say that you knew little, if anything, about what was going on?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yeah. I was certainly no expert. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you please pause between answer and question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It would be fair to say by the time you left you were no expert either?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yeah. I wouldn't be an expert, but I did know a lot more about the history of the area than when I came.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now that history, that knowledge that you learned, given that it would appear that from your own testimony, was spent primarily on the east side, would have been sort of from one of the warring factions; right?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes, but I also I lived on the west side. Our interpreter was Croatian, and most of the people when I was off duty that I socialised with and dealt with were Croatian people in Medjugorje. And they were always happy to try and tell me their side of what things were, so I actually got a good chance to listen to both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But when you were interacting with the folks in Medjugorje, those were civilian?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct. Civilian police, oh, yeah, and civilian people, and some -- yeah, mostly civilian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Whereas, on the east side, you were dealing with these military officers -- I mean, police officers; right?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct. But I did have -- I have a chance to speak to a number of civilians, some who had limited English, and we were able to communicate back and forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I got just a couple of topics. One is this convoy issue where it was stopped in East Mostar. Do you recall that incident; right?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes. You're referring to the one on the 25th of August?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 25th of August.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There you go. Now, I noticed, I was looking for it in your statement, and I didn't find it. I didn't find much, if anything, in there. Was there a particular reason why this was not prominently featured - in fact, it wasn't featured at all - into your statement?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Why "which" wasn't sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The fact that you had -- you were a participant in that event on August 25th.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes. I was a participant. I was there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I know but I don't see that in your statement. I don't see that anywhere where you, really, where you explain what was happening and why it happened in your statement. Was there a reason why that information was not given, or was it simply that whoever interviewed you was not interested in that information from you.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I think what he -- he had a copy of the report, the incident report, which basically explained everything, and he was going to use that for the information and it wasn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: -- necessary to have a detailed statement on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, today, on page 48, you told us what you believe were the reasons why that convoy was blocked, and you had indicated that it was Mr. Sorensen who had talked to Zuljevic; and from him, he had learned that there had been an HVO offensive, and that there would be another one coming.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, that was information that Mr. Sorensen then told you, and then you're telling us.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Sorensen didn't do any investigation to find out whether, in fact, what he had been told was actually correct.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I'm not sure he did any investigation on it or it would be possible for him to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't -- possibility another section, another -- I mean, but you don't know whether he made any efforts?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, but would it be fair to say if it came from Mr. Zuljevic, you would all, for intents and purposes accept, it as being true, accurate, and complete?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: Not at that time. I didn't know the man very well at that time. Later on, when I got to know him better, I felt that he was sincere and I would have -- after having known him for a while, I would have believed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But at that point, since nobody really knew him, it would at least be worthwhile to check and make sure whether Mr. Zuljevic was, in fact, being truthful at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: It would have been good to be able to do that, but it would be actually impossible to try and do a follow-up under those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. For -- well, you could ask him, for instance, where exactly did this incident take place? You could ask him that; right? And then, then, since there were lot of internationals around, SpaBat and others, you could then ask another question, maybe even three or four questions, and maybe find out whether an incident had occurred and had occurred in the manner in which it was being described to you by Mr. Zuljevic. That could have been do; right?

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: But you would still be in the same situation. Would you asking him questions and relying on his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: It was impossible to move around freely to actually go and check these things for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'm not asking about checking. I'm asking about, you know, asking other internationals that were there. All right. Now, I want to -- we may need to go into private session, Your Honour, because of the document, and it's P 01717?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I believe, I believe you were shown this morning a document, and it's 4511. This was generated by Mr. Sorensen, and I suspect that you are familiar with this document. It's a P document. It's a Prosecution document, 4511.

utterances.speaker: LARRY FORBES
utterances.text: I can look it up for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. It should be coming up shortly. If you don't have it, we'll give you a copy of it. But this was the document also that my colleague, Ms. Nozica, had asked you about.
